Remote work was supposed to mean more time for art, but it’s mostly meant more time for planning and less for actually drawing. 

I’m tired of feeling like I’m behind before the day begins. Every to-do list gets longer instead of shorter. I keep meaning to block out hours just for painting, but something always interrupts—a call, a delivery, some small task that can’t wait. I notice how my hands are shaking a bit, probably from not eating yet, or maybe just nerves. Tonight I want to finish that charcoal portrait, even if it means staying up late. I’m worried the result won’t match what I see in my head. Still, I know I’ll obsess over the details, erase and redraw. Sometimes I wonder if being so organized just adds to the pressure. Maybe if I was messier with my time, I’d find some freedom. For now, I’ll just rinse my cup and get started, hoping I can carve out a few hours for myself when the day is finally over.

persona.life_context: caring for a parent, stretched thin

journal_text: This morning, I was filling Dad’s pill organizer at the kitchen table, and realized I’d done it out of order again. The clock on the microwave said 6:13, but it felt much earlier. I could hear the refrigerator humming, louder than usual, or maybe that was just me. The cereal boxes were stacked unevenly on the counter, next to the crossword puzzle I’d half-finished last night. Dad shuffled in, asking if it was Saturday. I told him it was Thursday, but he looked at me blankly, so I just nodded and helped him sit down. The tea kettle whistled, and I actually jumped—my nerves are shot lately. I handed him his morning meds with a glass of water and tried to remember if I’d taken mine. There’s a heaviness in the kitchen, not just from the damp air, but from the routine itself. I keep thinking I should be able to manage this better, being a therapist, but the practical side of care is different than giving advice to others. I miss things—appointments, calls, sometimes meals. It’s hard to keep track. My mind feels thick, like everything is moving through molasses. Still, I caught myself hoping today would be a little smoother, maybe Dad will have a good day, maybe I’ll remember to eat lunch. I’m tired but trying to stay grounded. There’s no big insight, just the slow work of getting through the morning, one task at a time.

Feeling pretty drained this afternoon. Took a walk around the block just to clear my head after the last round of messages with Sam. The calendar is a mess again—school pick-ups, my studio time, her work shifts, and somehow everything overlaps. I tried to be blunt about what I need for next week, but it always feels like I’m asking for too much. The breeze was nice, at least, and there was a kid’s scooter abandoned on the sidewalk that made me think of how fast the kids are growing up. My phone buzzed again and I ignored it, not ready for another back-and-forth about who’s taking Thursday. I know we both want what’s best for the kids, but it’s like neither of us gets what we need. I keep telling myself we’re doing okay, but maybe I’m just trying to stay positive because the alternative is too heavy. My feet hurt and my mind’s jumping ahead to the next painting deadline. I wish I could just focus on one thing at a time. I watched a dog chase a ball across someone’s lawn and felt jealous for a second—how simple. I’m tired of always being the one to smooth things over. Maybe I’m just more tired than usual. Tomorrow I’ll try again to get the calendars sorted. Right now, I just want ten quiet minutes before the kids come home and it all starts up again.

The TV remote is wedged between the cushions again, just out of reach. Early sunlight is coming in through the half-closed blinds but it feels dim in here. She left for her office a couple hours ago, barely said goodbye. I think we both felt that tension, but I couldn’t quite figure out the right thing to say so I just stared at my phone.

My mind keeps jumping between yesterday’s argument and the endless job listings that I need to check. Working from home is supposed to be flexible but it mostly feels like I can’t escape any of it, work or home problems. I keep replaying what I said—maybe I was too abrupt? The silence in the house now just makes everything louder in my head. I wish I was better at talking things through instead of just letting them sit there, unresolved.

The quiet in here is just the soft hum of my laptop and the faint noise from cars making their way down the street. Light from the window comes in at an angle, making a stripe across the paperwork stacked on the desk. It’s almost 8:30, and I’m trying to keep my head clear before the day picks up speed.

This morning I had to double-check the shared calendar again, just to be sure about who’s picking up Mia from daycare tonight. There was a mix-up yesterday, and it turned into a frustrating text exchange with her dad. I tried to keep it factual and organized, but emotions always sneak in around the edges, even if I don’t type them out. We’re both trying to do what’s best for her, but sometimes it feels like every conversation is a negotiation. I don’t want things to be tense, especially since we have to coordinate so much. I keep hoping that if I stay calm and keep things structured, it’ll get easier over time. For now, I just want to get through today without another misunderstanding. The desk is already covered in color-coded notes, which gives me some sense of control. I know that’s not everything, but it helps. Time to get started on the day’s emails and see what else needs to be juggled before noon.

The parking lot lights are buzzing, those weird yellow halos, and I keep hearing the clank of carts getting dumped back in their stacks. Feels like the whole world is exhaling after a long day, but my head is just full of static. My phone keeps vibrating with unread messages from him, and I can’t decide if I want to read them or just toss my phone out the window. I’m so tired of this cycle—arguing, apologizing, promising things will change, and then we’re right back here like nothing moves forward. Maybe it’s partly my fault for overthinking every word and reading into silences, but tonight it felt like he was a million miles away, even when he was right next to me in the car.

I should be thinking about job applications, or at least about what I can make for dinner with the last $16 in my account, but my brain is foggy and all I can do is replay our conversation. Did I sound needy? Was I too harsh? I want closeness but I also want peace—I don’t know how to have both. It’s almost 7:30 and I’m just sitting here, watching people walk by with takeout bags, wishing I could just turn off my feelings for a night. The steering wheel is cold under my hands. I wish I could call Mom but I don’t want to burden her with this. Why is it so hard to just talk without it turning into some weird competition about who cares more or who’s more hurt? I keep checking the rearview mirror like I’m expecting someone else to show up and tell me what to do. Maybe I’ll just drive around a bit before heading home. Maybe he’ll text something different. Or maybe I’ll just ignore my phone for a while and try to remember what it felt like to breathe easy.

Managed to stretch the grocery money a bit further by skipping the pastry with my coffee this morning. The place is loud, but at least the refills are cheap if you ask. I’ve been running the numbers again on my phone, making sure I’m not missing any subscriptions I can cancel. There’s a couple at the next table talking about a ski trip—hard not to eavesdrop, but it’s not like I could go anywhere right now. I made a list of things that could bring in a little cash, but most require some up-front investment I just don’t have. The tile floor under my feet is cold, which I hadn’t noticed before, probably because I’m tired and not paying attention to much. I keep telling myself to stay spontaneous, look for small opportunities, but most days the energy isn’t there. Still, I crossed off three errands today, and that’s not nothing. Might pick up some discount bread on the way home and call it a win. The only thing left is to track today’s spending before I forget, again.

The steering wheel is still warm from the drive, my sketchbook propped up on the passenger seat, and there’s this weird satisfaction in stealing a few minutes away from the noise before I clock in tonight. I can hear the hum from the supermarket delivery trucks around the corner, and I keep tapping my fingers on my thigh, almost unconsciously, like I’m trying to keep pace with a song I don’t remember. The sun’s nearly down—orange light bouncing off the building across the lot, and I keep wondering if I’ll ever get used to these fragmented days, where I’m squeezing art between work shifts and roommate schedules and meal planning. My paints are still out back at the apartment, but I’ve got my pencil and a scrap of paper, and I keep scribbling ideas for that mural I’ve been obsessing over, even though I know I won’t touch it again until late tonight, maybe after midnight.

There’s something energizing about being this busy, even if my thoughts feel like they’re darting in every direction at once. I keep thinking about how I’ll probably forget to grab groceries again, because by the time I get home, my mind will already be on the next thing—did I remember to text back about that show next week? Did I leave my brushes soaking? The repetition of juggling my roommate’s calendar with my own, swapping nights for dishes, splitting fridge space, it’s a mess sometimes but I can’t imagine living totally alone. The chaos is weirdly comforting. I glance at the time—ten minutes before I have to go in. I wish I could freeze these little moments, just hang out in the quiet before everything picks up speed again. Maybe tonight I’ll finally finish that background layer, or maybe I’ll just end up doodling in the kitchen while my roommate reheats leftovers. Either way, it’s okay.

Just shoved my headphones into my ears after barely catching the bus, still thinking about that awkward conversation with Sarah at lunch. The rumble of the engine is making my brain feel even more jumbled, like I can’t land on one thought for more than a second. I wanted to explain what I meant about planning our weekend, but I kept tripping over my words and she looked so frustrated. Maybe I should have just listened instead of trying to fix everything right away. The bus is packed, people’s elbows everywhere, and all I can focus on is replaying what I said—or didn’t say—over and over. I keep worrying she took it as criticism, which wasn’t what I meant at all. Why is it so hard to just communicate what I’m actually feeling? I keep thinking if I was clearer, things would be easy, but my thoughts just scatter when it gets tense. There’s a guy across from me watching a video with the volume too loud, and I can’t even tune it out. Maybe I’ll text her when I get home and just say I’m sorry I was weird. I do want to get better at this, but some days it feels impossible. Wondering if anyone else on this bus is replaying their own conversations or if it’s just me lost in my head.

Had to check my bank app three times today, the numbers never get less depressing. Spent most of the night staring at the spreadsheet, trying to figure out what else I could cut—subscriptions, snacks, even the fancy toothpaste. It’s almost 1am now, whole apartment is quiet except for the fridge humming. Not sure if I’m more tired or just numb. Kept thinking about Mom—can’t believe it’s been almost a year since the diagnosis. The way she used to complain about grocery prices, guess I’m turning into her. I haven’t told anyone how much I worry about getting sick myself, can’t afford doctor visits, insurance is a joke. Sister texted a photo of Dad’s old chair, said she found it in storage, wants to know if I want it. Not sure I have space or energy to deal with that right now. My neck’s been stiff, probably from the way I sit hunched over the laptop, but I can’t help thinking it’s something worse. Almost skipped dinner but ate toast because I didn’t want to wake up dizzy. I should call my brother, been ignoring his messages. He keeps asking how I’m really doing, which just makes me want to avoid him more. Sometimes I wonder if anyone else worries about these things late at night or if it’s just me. Maybe I’ll feel better after some sleep, but I doubt it. Need to remember to buy more generic ibuprofen, and maybe look up free clinics just in case. The student loans are sitting there like a shadow. I keep telling myself I’ll get through this phase, but tonight doesn’t feel convincing. Going to try to sleep, even if my head won’t shut up. 🕰️

persona.life_context: new relationship, unsure where it is going

journal_text:
The glow from my laptop screen is the only thing keeping this room from going completely dark. I should be asleep, but my mind is full of tabs—some actual, some metaphorical. Today started at 7:23 AM with my phone alarm blaring far too close to my ear and a calendar reminder for three client calls, two invoices, and a note to send flowers to Mom. The mundane details are somehow comforting, even if they are relentless. The real distraction is the message I got from Mark this morning, which I’ve reread at least six times. It was funny, offbeat, and a little distant. Maybe he’s just busy, or maybe that’s optimism talking.

I keep asking myself if I’m reading too much into things, which, knowing me, is likely. The last time I tried to predict where a relationship was going, I ended up eating leftover lasagna alone for a week, so I’m not exactly trusting my instincts. Still, there’s hope buried under the sarcasm. Juggling deadlines used to be the main source of my stress, but now it’s mixed with this uncertainty about whether I want this relationship to go somewhere or if I’m just afraid of being alone. I can’t decide if I’m overthinking or just being practical. Maybe both. For now, I’ll just close some tabs—on the screen, at least.

Earlier today, I was checking my bank app on my phone, counting out what I’d have left after rent and groceries this week. It made me feel a bit anxious, but I told myself to just keep tracking every expense. Now, after dinner, I’m still at the table. The leftover rice is still in the pot, and I can hear the fridge humming in the corner. I’m tired, but my mind keeps replaying the conversation with Alex during the meal. She was frustrated about something work-related, but it felt like she was snapping at me for no reason. I tried to be gentle and just listen, but I think she took my quietness the wrong way. There was this awkward silence after she finished eating, and she didn’t look at me when she got up to wash her plate. I wanted to ask if she was okay, but the words didn’t come out. Instead, I just focused on scraping my own plate, which felt heavier than usual. I know things have been a bit tense between us lately, mostly because money is tight and we’re both stressed, but it’s hard not to take it personally sometimes. I keep wondering if I should have said more or tried to lighten the mood, but I just didn’t have the energy tonight. Now she’s in her room with the door closed, and I’m left at the table sorting receipts and thinking about what I could have done differently. It’s exhausting. I wish there was an easy way to reset things after these small arguments. For now, I’ll just finish my budget list and maybe text her in a bit, even though we’re just a few feet apart.

The metal prep table is cold under my hands, and the kitchen is too quiet for how much I know I have to do tonight. I got here early hoping the stillness would help me sort my thoughts, but it’s just made them louder. I keep glancing at the list taped to the fridge—so many things to prep, sauces to finish, desserts to plate. My mind keeps jumping ahead, worrying if I’ll get it all done before service. Breathing feels shallow, like I’m always two steps behind even when it’s only me here. I caught myself slicing onions too fast and had to stop, wipe my eyes, remind myself to slow down. It’s just one day, one dinner service, but sometimes the weight of it all sits heavy, and I wonder if I’m missing something important. The hum of the fridge is steady, at least, and the first light is coming in through the window. I hope when the rest of the team arrives, their energy will help me shake this feeling. For now, I just need to start with one task and trust it will come together. I wish I could call someone just to talk, but everyone I know is asleep. Maybe that’s okay. Maybe I just need a few quiet minutes to get my head right before it all starts.

Earlier this morning, I found Mom’s old photo stuck in one of my unpacked books—her smile, that knitted blue sweater. I think I just sat there on the floor for a few minutes, book in one hand, photo in the other, wishing I could call her. Now it’s almost dusk, walking around the block, hands shoved deep in my jacket because I forgot gloves. The trees here aren’t the same as back home, more maples, less pine—still adjusting, or not adjusting, not sure which. My chest still tight from the news last week, the doctor’s voice echoing in my head. I keep replaying the conversation, searching for something I missed or misunderstood. The cold air helps a bit, but my mind feels jumpy, skipping from work emails I haven’t answered to the casserole dish I can’t find since the move. Passing the neighbor’s dog barking at the fence, I force a smile. I want to feel settled, but it’s like my body’s here and my head is somewhere else, maybe back in my old kitchen, or at the hospital, or just nowhere. I keep telling myself a routine will help. Maybe tomorrow I’ll finally unpack the last box. For now, I just keep walking, hoping to feel more like myself with each step.

persona.life_context: new city, still building a social circle

journal_text: This morning, I tried to crack eggs one-handed like I saw on YouTube—ended up with more shell in the bowl than out. I laughed, but the prep guy just stared at me like I’d lost my mind. Fast forward to now: I’m huddled at a tiny table in the storage room, lunch break in full swing, chewing on cold pasta and avoiding eye contact with everyone else cycling through. It still feels like everyone’s got their own little cliques and in-jokes that I can’t quite catch up to, which is honestly exhausting. I wanted to ask if anyone wanted to grab a drink after work but chickened out again, worrying I’d just come off as desperate or awkward. The city’s loud and busy but the kitchen is its own universe—sometimes I feel more invisible there than on the packed subway. My hands still smell faintly of garlic and burnt toast. I keep trying to make casual conversation, but the words always tumble out weird or too fast, and then there’s this silence. Maybe it’s just early days, or maybe I’m just bad at this. Either way, I’m counting down the minutes until I can go home and not have to think about impressing anyone at all. Tomorrow, maybe I’ll risk the egg trick again, but probably not in public.

Have to remember to buy more eggs, nearly dropped the last one when I was trying to juggle making toast and answering that email from work at 6:43am. Light in the kitchen is too bright this morning, kind of hurts my eyes but I don’t feel like fussing with the switch. Kept thinking about Dad’s old mug as I poured the coffee, still can’t bring myself to use it since last winter. Stupid how an object can make things sting again, I guess.

My mind keeps bouncing from bills to Mom’s next checkup to whether I sent that document to the client or not, and then back to memories. The house feels really quiet today, almost like it’s waiting for something. I’m restless, keep opening drawers or looking out the window just to do something with my hands. Thought about calling my sister but I know it’s early and she probably doesn’t want to talk about hospital visits before breakfast. I keep telling myself I should have visited more last year, even though I know it wouldn’t have changed anything. Hard not to replay.

I left my shoes by the fridge again, which makes no sense, but that’s just how my morning brain works. Going to try to make a list for today but I know I’ll lose it or forget what was on it. Still, got to keep moving, even if it feels like I’m only half-there most mornings lately. Maybe I’ll go for a walk before work starts, just to clear my head a bit. Or maybe I’ll just sit here and watch the toaster for a while. Haven’t decided yet.

persona.life_context: caring for a parent, stretched thin

journal_text: Feeling a little on edge but mostly determined as I stand in the kitchen before my shift. The house is quiet except for the humming of the fridge and the distant sound of someone moving upstairs—probably Mom, awake earlier than usual. The sunlight is just starting to filter in through the blinds, making everything look a bit softer. I made some toast and tea, just something quick, because I know the afternoon will be packed. I keep thinking about the customer returns I have to process today, and whether I’ll have time to drop off Mom’s prescription on my lunch break. Balancing work and caring for her is exhausting, but somehow I’m managing to keep up with it all. I keep going over my to-do list in my head, making sure I don’t forget anything. My mind keeps jumping from one task to the next, almost like I can’t stop planning every minute. I try to remember to breathe and eat, even when I feel like I can’t slow down. Being patient with myself is harder than being patient with customers, honestly. Still, I’m grateful for the small moments of quiet, like this one, where I can just stand still and listen. I know this afternoon will be busy, but I feel ready to handle it. As long as I keep focusing on one thing at a time, I think I can get through it all. I just wish there were more hours in the day. I’m hopeful, though—maybe I’ll even have a few minutes to read after work if Mom is feeling okay. For now, it’s just me, my tea, and the sunlight sneaking across the counter.

Today I realized my grocery budget is basically just an exercise in self-delusion. I spent half an hour comparing prices of different brands of oatmeal and still ended up buying the one on sale that tastes like cardboard. There’s something weird about standing in a fluorescent-lit aisle at 10:30 pm, mentally calculating how many meals I can stretch out of a single can of beans. Maybe that’s adulthood? Or maybe I’m just bad at spreadsheets. I keep telling myself this is temporary, but the whole "tighten your belt" thing is not exactly inspiring. Lying here with my laptop open, reading about people who quit their jobs to travel the world, and meanwhile I’m just trying to figure out if I can afford the extra data plan. Honestly, I don’t even know what I’d do if money wasn’t an issue. Probably still overthink which brand of oatmeal to buy. At least the apartment is quiet. The hum from my old fridge is weirdly comforting tonight.

persona.life_context: in school, balancing work and classes

journal_text: Closed my laptop a minute ago after hammering out a mediocre draft for tomorrow’s research meeting, but my brain is still compulsively cycling through what happened with Anna earlier. Sunlight is coming in at a weird angle through the blinds, making little stripes across the mess of papers and half-drunk tea mugs on the coffee table—somehow that feels like my whole afternoon: fragmented, busy, but still not adding up to anything coherent. She texted around noon, asking if I actually wanted to talk or just keep pushing things off until "after finals" (which, as she pointed out, is a moving target). I tried to explain I’m not avoiding her, but it sounded defensive even to me. Between the TA gig, classes, and my thesis committee’s never-ending demands, I honestly don’t know how people make time for relationships without something imploding. Still, I feel lousy knowing she thinks I don’t care when the truth is I just don’t have enough bandwidth. Maybe I should’ve just called her instead of overthinking my replies and letting the conversation fizzle awkwardly. Now I keep replaying what I could have said that would have sounded less like an excuse and more like the truth. My phone buzzed with a reminder about a group meeting, but it just made me want to throw it across the room. I know I’m supposed to be grateful for opportunities, but right now everything feels like a juggling act where every ball is coated in oil. I should probably eat something before my next Zoom call, but the kitchen is a disaster and the idea of doing both life and work well seems laughable. Maybe I’ll text Anna again, or maybe I’ll just stare at the ceiling for a while and hope clarity arrives in the form of a lightning bolt. Honestly, I’d settle for a nap at this point.

Mostly feeling flat today, not in a bad way, just sort of hovering in neutral. I ended up at the coffee shop down the street, partly because my new apartment still feels like someone else’s space and partly because I needed Wi-Fi that actually works. There’s this quiet hum of people typing and cups clinking, which is almost comforting at this point. My phone buzzed a few times with reminders for different errands—utilities still need to be sorted out, and something about renter’s insurance, which I keep forgetting. The to-do list feels longer than it should be for a single person, and every time I cross off one thing, two more seem to appear. I keep thinking I should feel more settled by now, but the boxes in my living room are a constant reminder that I’m not. I tried to tackle some reading for class but kept getting distracted by little details, like the chipped paint on the table and the way the sunlight moves across the floor here. It’s weird to feel so detached from the city, like I’m just visiting instead of living here. At the same time, there’s a small part of me that’s excited about the possibilities, even if that feeling is mostly buried under the logistics. I caught myself daydreaming about what this place will feel like in a few months—maybe I’ll have a favorite spot, maybe this coffee shop will be it. For now, I’m just trying to keep up with daily tasks and not overthink the bigger picture. Maybe that’s enough. The afternoon is creeping by, and I’ll probably head home soon to unpack a few more things. Hopefully tomorrow the apartment will feel a little more like mine.

This morning, I woke up to the sound of my phone buzzing on the nightstand again—another group text from the lab team, already arguing about who’s taking the lead on the new sample protocols. Half awake, I scrolled through the messages, rolling my eyes at how quickly it turned into a passive-aggressive mess. I made a mental note to avoid replying until after breakfast, otherwise I’d get sucked into the drama before even brushing my teeth. Now it’s about 10:15 AM and I’m on the couch, laptop open, receipts and a spreadsheet spread out in front of me. The numbers don’t lie—groceries are up, rent is due in four days, and I can’t ignore the fact that I’m barely scraping by this month. I keep thinking about how easily the lab team gets into arguments over the smallest things, like who cleans the glassware or who left unlabeled tubes in the fridge. I try to stay organized and keep my head down, but it’s getting harder to ignore the tension. It’s not that I expect everyone to get along, but the constant sniping is exhausting, especially when I have to double-check everyone’s data because I’m skeptical about their shortcuts. I’m nervous about bringing up my concerns in the next meeting; I know I’ll probably sound blunt, but someone has to say something if we want to publish anything decent. The couch cushions are lumpy, my back aches, and my coffee’s gone cold, but I can’t seem to get up. I keep rereading the last email from my supervisor, trying to figure out if there’s a hidden message about my performance. Part of me wonders if I’m just overthinking it, but the other part knows I’m probably right. I wish I could just focus on my own work without getting dragged into everyone else’s drama. At least I’ve got my color-coded expense tracker—small victories where I can find them. Maybe after lunch, I’ll finally reply to those texts and try to steer things back on track. Or maybe not. Either way, I’m tired of feeling like I’m the only one paying attention to the details that actually matter.

Closed the fridge door a minute ago, having just grabbed the last yogurt. The sun barely comes through the tiny window above the sink at this hour, just enough to remind me that I should have slept more. I stood there for a while listening to the hum of the refrigerator, thinking about the string of messages I need to answer this afternoon—clients waiting for updates, a couple of invoices still hanging in limbo. I don’t know why, but the more work comes in, the more I feel like I’m getting away with something. Maybe that’s just freelancing: never quite sure if you’re busy or just scrambling.

My to-do list is already half-scrawled on a sticky note stuck to the microwave, and I keep glancing at it as if it’s going to rearrange itself. It’s oddly satisfying when small things get crossed off, though. Still, I can’t help but worry about whether this streak of steady projects is going to dry up. There’s a weird comfort in the chaos, but it’s also exhausting. I’ll try to get a run in before noon to clear my head, but for now, I’m just hoping the rest of today goes as planned and that nobody throws me a curveball. At least breakfast is sorted, even if everything else isn’t.

persona.life_context: new city, still building a social circle

journal_text: I missed the earlier bus because I couldn’t find my wallet, so by the time I finally got on, it was almost midnight and the city lights outside looked blurry through the window. I kept replaying the conversation with Julia from earlier in the evening, trying to figure out if I’d said the wrong thing or if she was just tired. She seemed distant, distracted, and when I asked if everything was okay, she just shrugged and looked away. I know we’re both adjusting to new routines here, but I can’t help but wonder if I’m just not doing enough to connect with her, or if maybe it’s something else entirely. The bus was half-empty, and some guy in the back was snoring loudly, which made it even harder to focus on my thoughts. My phone buzzed with a message, but it was just a spam alert, not the apology or explanation I half-hoped for. The city feels bigger and more impersonal at this hour, and I still don’t have anyone I’d call for a late-night talk. Maybe I’m overanalyzing things, but I keep thinking about what I could have said differently. The orange streetlights flickered as we stopped at a red light, and I caught my own reflection in the glass—tired, a bit older-looking than I remember. Finding a job is stressful enough, but feeling like I have to rebuild trust or understanding with someone I care about adds another layer. I guess I just want to feel settled, both with work and with the people closest to me. For now, though, all I can do is get home, try to sleep, and hope tomorrow brings a bit more clarity.

persona.life_context: new city, still building a social circle

journal_text: I spent most of yesterday evening adjusting the lighting in my studio area yet again, as the shadows on the new canvas just weren’t cooperating. By the time I finally called it quits, it was past midnight and I ended up sprawled on the living room couch, half-watching the city lights flicker through the window. I can’t help but feel the weight of the upcoming gallery submission deadline pressing in on me—there’s a constant internal debate between pushing for technical perfection and just letting the work breathe as it wants to. The unfamiliarity of this city is still gnawing at me; I miss having someone to bounce ideas off of, or even just a familiar face to decompress with after a long session. My hands smelled faintly of oil paint and turpentine, and I noticed a streak of blue on my wrist I must have missed. The silence here is both comforting and unsettling; it gives me space to focus, but sometimes I catch myself wishing for the ambient noise of my old neighborhood. I drafted out a rough plan for tomorrow’s work, but I’ve been second-guessing every decision, right down to the type of brush I’ll use. Maybe it’s just fatigue, or maybe the pressure is getting under my skin more than I want to admit. I know I’m good at what I do, but the constant need to prove it in a new environment is exhausting. The couch felt lumpy but familiar by now; I stared at the ceiling for a while, trying to settle my thoughts, before finally forcing myself to get some sleep.

Today I spent at least twenty minutes looking for the box with the kitchen towels, only to find it under a pile of winter coats by the front door. I swore I’d be more organized after the move, but it’s like every system I try to set up gets interrupted by a crying baby, a spilled snack, or just my own wandering attention. The living room still smells faintly of cardboard, and the couch is lumpy because I haven’t found the right cushions yet. It’s early afternoon, and there’s a patch of sunlight on the rug that I keep staring at while I think about what this place is supposed to be for us. I keep wondering when this house will feel like home, or if that’s even something that just happens on its own. Sometimes I feel like I’m playing house rather than actually living in it—especially when I catch myself making mental lists of what I should be doing instead of just being present with my kid. There’s a weird kind of calm here, almost like I’m waiting for some switch to flip so I can settle in for real. I know I’m supposed to be grateful for the fresh start, and I am, but the uncertainty about pretty much everything makes me restless. My mind keeps drifting to who I was before becoming a mom and before this move, and whether I’ll ever feel grounded again. Even now, with laundry still unfolded and dishes in the sink, I’m analyzing what needs doing next instead of actually doing it. Maybe that’s just the way my brain works, but it’s exhausting at times. I hope that soon, the chaos will fade and I’ll find a rhythm here that finally feels like mine.

The bus engine is louder than usual this morning, and there’s a flicker of sunlight through the dirty window. I keep checking my phone, scrolling through emails that I don’t want to answer yet. My mind is foggy. Last night I was up late debugging a client’s code and now I can’t focus on anything for more than a few seconds. The bus bumps over a pothole and I almost drop my laptop bag. There’s a crumpled receipt under my shoe that I can’t remember getting.

Freelance income is a mess right now. I have three clients, but only one paid me on time this month. I keep thinking I should find something more stable, maybe a part-time contract, but I like being on my own schedule. Still, the uncertainty is making it hard to concentrate on the actual work. Deadlines are stacking up. I tried making a list of priorities, but everything feels equally urgent. I need to send two invoices, finish a bug fix, and somehow plan my week before noon. The bus is almost at my stop, but I’m not sure if I’m ready to face another day of endless small tasks. It’s hard to keep track of what matters when every job feels like it might be the last.

Earlier this morning, I had to hunt for my keys for a solid ten minutes, which made me late for the pharmacy pickup, and I still can’t remember where I finally found them. Now I’m wedged into this corner seat at the coffee shop, half-listening to the espresso machine hiss and trying to make sense of the overloaded to-do list in my planner. It’s only mid-morning and already my phone is buzzing with reminders—doctor’s appointment for Mom, groceries (we’re out of eggs and somehow also out of milk again?), plus I need to check in with Mark about dinner. I feel like I’m juggling a dozen things at once, and every time I cross something off, two more pop up. My mind’s jumping between the next thing and the last thing I forgot, and I keep getting distracted by the music playing overhead. I want to just breathe for a second but I keep thinking I’ll forget something important if I relax.

Mark and I haven’t really talked properly this week—just quick logistical check-ins and reminders, nothing meaningful. I know we said we’d try to work on that, but it’s so hard to find the energy when my brain’s fried by noon. Maybe if I write all this down, it’ll clear some space? I’m not sure, but I’ve got to try something before I burn out completely.

This morning, I was standing in the kitchen, staring at my phone as I checked my email for the third time in twenty minutes. There was nothing new, just the same rejection from yesterday and some spam about online courses. I remember how the countertop felt cool under my hands. Now, a few hours later, I’m walking around the block just trying to shake off this restless energy. The air smells a bit like cut grass, and there’s a kid a few doors down bouncing a basketball against the curb. I keep thinking about the proposal I sent out last week—maybe I should have phrased things differently, or made my portfolio look sharper. My mind keeps circling back to all the places I might have gone wrong, and I can’t help but wonder if I’m missing something obvious that everyone else knows. I keep telling myself that freelancing has always been unpredictable, but lately, the gaps between gigs feel longer and more nerve-wracking. My shoes are rubbing against my heel, and even that small discomfort makes me more irritable. I keep glancing at my phone, half-hoping for some notification—anything, really—but it’s just silent. Every time I try to reassure myself, it doesn’t stick for long. I know I need to keep pushing, but the anxiety feels like it’s always just under the surface, waiting to trip me up. I wish I had a better way to get out of my head on days like this.

Feel a bit tense, a little on edge, but also kind of hopeful. Early morning again, standing in the kitchen and trying to get the kettle to boil faster, like that’ll help me get ahead. The counter is cluttered–mail, half-eaten banana, grocery list from last week I never finished. Sun is barely coming in through the window, just this weak strip of light across the fridge. My phone keeps buzzing, probably reminders for invoices or messages from clients about deadlines. I keep telling myself it’s fine, that the work will come, but this week’s been so up and down. One client bailed last minute, and another one wants a rush job, so I’m scrambling to fit everything in before noon. 

Had a weird argument with my partner last night, nothing big but it stuck with me. She says I always seem distracted, like I’m not really here when we’re talking. Maybe I am, I don’t know. I want to explain how the pressure gets to me sometimes, how I’m always thinking ahead, worrying about next week’s bills, but I don’t want to sound like I’m making excuses. She left early this morning, barely said anything. I know I need to make it right, maybe send her a message before I get lost in work. I keep thinking I’ll get better at balancing everything, but it always feels like I’m rushing through the day, just barely keeping up. Need to find a way to slow down, at least for a minute, before the emails start piling up. Maybe after breakfast, if I can remember to eat.

This morning I found myself staring at the pill organizer by the sink, just counting through the compartments for Mom, making sure I didn’t miss anything even though I’ve checked it three times already. Felt like it set the tone for the day—always double checking, triple checking. Now, after dinner, the kitchen is still a mess. There’s a half-eaten plate of lasagna, my laptop open next to a bottle of Tylenol, and I keep thinking about how much I hate that work emails are coming in even now, when all I want is a few quiet minutes with my thoughts.

I keep hearing the hum of the dishwasher and the clink of someone’s fork, but my mind drifts to Dad, how he used to clear the table with this big showy sigh like he was the only one who could do it right. It’s hard not to feel the gap he left, especially when things get quiet. I try to be hopeful, I really do, and I keep the family calendar updated and the to-do lists on my phone, but these days feel like they’re piling up faster than I can sort them. Even organizing things doesn’t bring the relief it used to. I know tomorrow will bring more of the same, but maybe I’ll find a way to carve out an hour for myself. For now, I’ll just sit here and listen to the dishwasher until it’s done.

The morning sun is sharp through the windshield, making it hard to look up from the steering wheel. Cars keep pulling in and slamming doors. I’m early, but my hands are restless on my lap. I keep thinking about mom’s last hospital visit, about how fragile her voice sounded on the phone. Work feels pointless when these things are happening at home, but I’m supposed to show up for other people. My laptop bag is on the passenger seat, spilling out files I haven’t touched. I wish I could call my brother but I don’t know what I’d say; we never talk about this directly. I’ll take a few more breaths, maybe text him later, and then go inside.

This afternoon, I kept replaying that moment in the grocery store when I caught myself reaching for the same brand of cereal he always bought, and then stopped—almost dropped the box. It’s strange how little things like that can just catch me off guard. At the time, it felt like someone pressed pause on everything else and I was just standing there, holding this dumb box and feeling out of place. Now, after dinner, I’m still at the table, staring at a half-empty glass of water and the stack of unopened mail next to it, feeling the weight of it all. The apartment is too quiet except for the hum of the fridge, and I keep wishing I could just call someone—maybe him, maybe not—but I can’t decide what I’d even say.

We barely spoke at lunch. There was this tension, like neither of us knew what to talk about, or maybe we were both avoiding the things we really needed to say. I keep wondering if it’s just the move, or if it’s me—maybe I’m too restless, too uncertain about where I fit now. I used to feel so sure about everything, but lately I second-guess myself about the smallest things. I can’t seem to settle, can’t distract myself with work the way I used to. Even washing the dishes tonight felt like some big effort. I know I’m supposed to give it time, but I’m impatient, I guess. I just want to feel like myself again, or at least figure out who that is here. Maybe I’ll go for a walk before bed, even if it’s dark—at least it’s something to do.

persona.life_context: in school, balancing work and classes

journal_text:
Sunlight is barely creeping through the blinds, and the fridge hums louder than usual in the quiet of the kitchen. My tea is steeping, but I’m barely paying attention to it, already making a mental checklist for the day and feeling like I’m ten steps behind. There’s so much to juggle—work deadlines, assignments due, group project meetings that I dread because it’s always awkward to coordinate with classmates who seem so much younger or just on a different wavelength. I try to stay positive and remind myself that I’ve pulled off worse, but lately, every little interaction feels like one more thing to analyze and worry about. Did I sound too bossy last night in the chat? Am I coming off as distant at work because I keep checking my phone for school notifications? It’s hard not to spiral when I’m stretched thin and everything feels urgent.

I know I should be grateful for these opportunities, and most days I am, but today it’s all just a bit much. The calendar on the fridge is full of scribbles—appointments, class times, reminders to call people back that I keep ignoring. I’ve noticed I’m getting snappier with people around me, and I hate that. I want to be approachable and calm, but all the multitasking leaves me short-tempered and scattered. Maybe if I focus on just getting through the next task, things will start to feel manageable again. Or maybe I just need a real breakfast and a moment to breathe. For now, I’ll just sip my tea and watch the light get a little brighter, hoping I’ll figure out how to connect with people without feeling like it’s all falling apart.

persona.life_context: new relationship, unsure where it is going

journal_text: Plastic fork in one hand, salad in the other, my phone screen lighting up with unread messages from her. Lunch break is strangely quiet, just the hum of the old fridge in the staff room and the occasional rattle from the vending machine. I keep thinking about last night—her voice was softer than usual, not angry, but something off. She asked where I thought this was going. I didn’t answer right away. I said I was tired, which was true, but also a way out. I stared at the ceiling after we hung up, tracing the cracks, listening to the faint traffic outside my window. Not sure who I’m supposed to be in this relationship, or if I even know what I want out of it. Part of me wants to just let it ride and see what happens. Another part wants to hit pause and figure myself out first. She joked about my "mystery" this morning, but I could tell she meant it. Being private is easier than being honest, at least for me. Maybe I’m just not ready to let anyone in all the way. Focused on work now, but the questions keep looping in the background like a bad song on repeat. I wish I had a better answer for both of us.

This morning, I found myself staring at the Google calendar on my phone before I’d even had breakfast, trying to remember if I’d already confirmed tomorrow’s drop-off with Mark. I thought I had, but then my mind started spinning about whether I’d forgotten to update him about the dentist appointment next week. It feels like every day is just a stream of reminders and adjustments, and I’m always worried something will fall through the cracks. Now it’s almost 8pm, and I’m slumped on the couch, laptop open but untouched, because I can’t bring myself to look at job postings right now. The living room is a mess—socks everywhere, a half-eaten apple on the coffee table, and I keep hearing the dryer spin in the background. I keep telling myself I should be applying to at least three jobs a day, but the whole process feels pointless lately. All these job descriptions asking for skills I barely remember having, or weirdly specific software I’ve never even heard of. I know I’m supposed to stay organized, and I have a spreadsheet for applications, but it’s honestly just making me feel more overwhelmed. I feel guilty for not being more productive, especially when I think about setting an example for the kids. Part of me wonders if I’m just making excuses, but then I start doubting whether any of this effort will actually pay off. Mark texted me again about switching weekends, and I wanted to say no, but I can already see the calendar dominoes falling if I don’t agree. I hate that my schedule is always up for negotiation and I never get to plan more than a week ahead. I’m tired—like, bone-deep tired—and still can’t turn off the part of my brain that’s buzzing about what I might be missing. Maybe tomorrow I’ll actually apply for something, or maybe I’ll just reorganize the spreadsheet again. I wish I could just stop worrying for five minutes.

persona.life_context: caring for a parent, stretched thin

journal_text: The dishwasher is humming in the background and there’s a faint clatter every so often as plates shift. I’m at the table, dinner cleared, but I can’t quite get up yet. I keep glancing at Mom’s pill organizer—tonight she seemed extra tired, barely touched her soup. It’s hard not to worry, but I’ve gotten good at hiding it from her. I’m supposed to be checking work emails, but my laptop is just sitting open, untouched; my brain is spinning through lists anyway. Groceries, meds, code reviews, laundry, doctor’s appointment reminders—everything jumbled together. I wish I could just focus on one thing at a time, but that’s not life right now. Still, I try to keep everything mapped out in my planner, even if it’s mostly crossed out and rewritten. I caught myself snapping at Dad earlier over something tiny, which makes me feel guilty now. I want to be patient, but sometimes I run out. The kitchen light is too bright, but I’m too restless to move. Maybe I’ll just make some tea and look out the window for a minute before I tackle the rest of the night.

The overhead lights on the bus flickered every so often, making the whole aisle feel unsteady, and the constant hum of tires on wet pavement made my head buzz. It was almost midnight and I was just staring out the foggy window, my backpack digging into my shoulder and my phone almost out of battery. I kept replaying the argument with my roommate from earlier—how the kitchen was a mess again and how neither of us could find time to clean it. It’s not even that big of a deal, but every little thing seems bigger when I’m running on five hours of sleep and too many deadlines. My brain felt so full, like there was no room left for kindness, even though I know I want to be understanding. I think maybe we’re both just stretched thin with our schedules; she’s working late shifts, I’m on-call for these never-ending sprints at work, and the apartment feels more like a train station than a home lately. I hate that I snapped at her, but at the same time, I wish she could see how overwhelmed I am too. Sometimes I wonder if we’re just talking past each other, both desperate for the other to notice how hard we’re trying. The bus jerked to a stop and I almost dropped my laptop bag—my hands were shaking, which I didn’t even notice until then. I keep telling myself tomorrow will be better, that maybe if we sit down and talk we’ll figure out a way to make things work. But right now, everything feels so heavy and complicated. The city lights outside blurred into streaks as we sped past, and I just wanted to get home, put on my headphones, and forget about people for a little while. Maybe I’ll text her in the morning. Or maybe I’ll just let things cool off. Either way, I really hope we can find a way to make this place feel lighter again.

Just finished a long conversation with Alex about how we've been missing each other’s signals lately, and now I’m sprawled out on the couch, feeling the late evening chill even with the blanket pulled up. The TV is flickering in the background, but I can’t focus on it—my mind keeps replaying little moments from the day, wondering if I could have handled things differently. We’re both trying, but sometimes it seems like every attempt at clarity just adds another layer of confusion. I know I have a tendency to react quickly, sometimes to fill the silence or just because I want to keep things moving. Today, I tried to hold back and listen, but I caught myself zoning out halfway through his explanation, probably because I’m so tired. There’s this nagging restlessness in me, pushing me to want to fix everything right now, but patience is supposed to be my strong suit. I caught myself fiddling with the throw pillow, tracing the threads, as he talked about how overwhelmed he’s been at work. I get it, but I also wish he’d ask about my day without me having to prompt him. On the other hand, maybe I haven’t made enough space for that, either. It’s weird how being hopeful for us sometimes feels at odds with being honest—like I’m afraid to admit things still feel a little off. I’m trying to remind myself that progress isn’t always obvious, and small steps still count. For now, I’m going to let the noise of the TV wash over me and hope tomorrow feels a bit lighter.

I realized halfway through my shift that I'd forgotten to pack a snack again. It’s strange how tiny routines like that start slipping when everything else feels unsettled. The bus is humming, almost empty, and I keep tapping my fingers against the seat, trying to remember the last time I felt truly rooted somewhere. The city is still unfamiliar—every street looks similar, but none of them hold any memories for me yet.

I keep wondering what it means to feel at home. Is it just about time, or is there something else I should be doing to settle in? The regulars at the café have started to recognize me, but I’m not sure I’ve recognized myself lately. My mind drifts back to earlier, weighing whether I’m just going through the motions or actively shaping something here. Maybe I’m overthinking it, but the uncertainty feels persistent.

The sun is starting to set, casting those long shadows through the dirty bus windows. The driver’s radio is playing some old pop song, muffled and tinny, almost comforting in its predictability. I’m calm, but there’s this undercurrent of restlessness. The move was supposed to be a fresh start, but so far it’s just made me more aware of the gaps in my day and the way I fill them.

I know I’m patient, or at least people tell me I am, but I don’t know how that helps when it comes to figuring out who I am in a new place. Maybe I’ll try a new route home tomorrow, or stop by the park before work. Small steps, I guess. For now, I’ll just watch the city pass by and hope that these small choices add up to something that feels like belonging eventually.

Feeling unsettled tonight. Dinner just finished and everyone scattered quickly, leaving plates, stray napkins, and a half-empty salad bowl on the table. The clatter of forks and the hum of conversation faded too soon, replaced by the muffled sounds of TV from the living room. I lingered at the table longer than usual, hoping for a quieter moment with my partner, but she seemed preoccupied, tapping away at her phone and barely looking up. It’s been tense between us this week, small misunderstandings piling up into something heavier. I wish I knew how to break through the awkwardness, but every attempt feels forced and awkward, so I hold back more than I should.

I sometimes wonder if I’m drifting away from the person I thought I was—someone open and spontaneous, eager to connect. Lately, I don’t recognize myself; I second-guess what to say, how to make things better without creating more distance. Maybe this is what happens when privacy is so hard to come by and everyone’s schedules keep colliding instead of syncing. I have the urge to just pack up my notebook and write somewhere else, but I know that’s escaping, not solving. For now, I’ll settle for jotting these thoughts down here, hoping tomorrow brings a lighter mood.

journal_text: The clock on the microwave keeps blinking 12:36 and I still haven’t fixed it since the power flickered last week—somehow that feels like a metaphor for today. I made tea this afternoon, trying to shake the fog from my head, but the exhaustion just settled deeper behind my eyes, like I’m running on fumes and stubbornness. The person I’m seeing texted me mid-shift to ask if I wanted to meet for a walk, and I wanted to say yes but I had three appointments stacked and then Mrs. Turner's son called to reschedule, so my whole afternoon was a blur of calendars and reminders and writing things on sticky notes I’ll probably misplace. I keep catching myself thinking about this new relationship, trying to figure out if it’s actually going anywhere or if we’re both just kind of floating along because it’s easier than being alone. I can’t tell if I’m being too cautious or not cautious enough—sometimes I think I should just ask them outright what they want but then I get shy and end up talking about their dog instead. The house is so quiet now except for the hum of the fridge, and I keep replaying little moments from earlier: the way my client smiled when I remembered her favorite sweater, or the way I couldn’t quite look my date in the eye when we talked about plans for next week. I feel like I’m always taking care of someone, making sure other people are okay, but who’s looking out for me? I wish I could turn off the part of my brain that worries about whether I’m doing enough, being enough, saying the right thing. I think about what it would feel like to let someone take care of me for a change, then immediately feel guilty for even wanting that. The laundry basket is overflowing again—somehow laundry always feels like the last straw. Maybe tomorrow I’ll fix the clock. Or maybe it can just keep blinking for a while, reminding me that time keeps moving whether I’m ready or not.

I woke up late again today, which meant I had to rush through making breakfast for Mom and I barely had time to check her meds. The pill organizer is missing Wednesday and Thursday—did I forget to refill those or did she take them already? I can’t even remember what day it is half the time. The living room is a mess; there are magazines and blankets everywhere, and I keep tripping over her slippers near the couch. I swear, every time I get a moment to myself, there’s a new thing I realize I forgot—doctor’s appointments, groceries, laundry piling up. I started making a to-do list on my phone but then I misplaced the phone under a cushion and spent twenty minutes looking for it. I know I should ask for more help, but it feels like I’m the only one who knows how to keep things going. My partner tries, I know he does, but I get so frustrated when he leaves things half-finished or doesn’t listen to what I’m actually asking. We keep promising to talk more, to actually sit down and have a conversation, but it never seems to happen because there’s always something urgent. I snapped at him about the bills this morning, which I regret, but sometimes I don’t even realize how tense I am until I hear my own voice. The TV was blaring some morning show in the background, and I couldn’t even focus on what I was saying. I miss having just a few minutes of quiet, where I don’t have to think about anyone else’s needs. Maybe I’ll try to get out for a walk later, if I can sneak away for half an hour. Right now, I just want to sit here and not move for a bit, but there’s still so much to do. The sun is coming through the window, and for a second it actually felt peaceful, until the phone rang again. I wish I could keep that peaceful feeling for longer than a few seconds at a time.

My laptop fan is buzzing again, sounding way too loud for this hour—it's 11:30 pm and the only other noise is the streetlight flickering outside my window. I keep glancing at my phone, even though there’s nothing new; the group chat is dead and I muted notifications anyway. I’ve spent most of today at this same desk, halfheartedly searching job sites or reading articles about remote work burnout. Technically, I’m not working, but I feel like I never stop working—just obsessing over what I’m supposed to be doing or who I’m supposed to become. The line between my own goals and what other people expect is getting so blurry. I caught myself snapping at my partner earlier, something about the dishes, but really I was just frustrated with myself. I apologized but it felt awkward, like we’re both avoiding the real conversation about how stuck I feel. Every time I try to map out a plan, my thoughts scatter—one minute I’m considering a coding bootcamp, the next I’m thinking about moving to a new city, then I just lose all focus and scroll social media instead. My head is tired but I can’t shut it down. Sometimes I wonder if I’m even cut out for any of these remote opportunities or if I’m just floating because I’m too scared to commit to anything real. The worst part is I don’t even know what I want, only what I don’t want. My partner says I overthink everything, but how else am I supposed to figure myself out? There’s a pile of laundry on the chair and I can’t even manage to put it away tonight. Maybe tomorrow I’ll wake up with more clarity, but I’m not counting on it.

This morning I dropped my pen in the elevator and watched it roll right into the crack by the door, typical start. Now it’s almost midnight and I can still feel the stupid ache in my shoulders from hunching over my laptop all day. The living room’s a mess—sketches everywhere, empty cup noodles from dinner, and I’m too tired to care or clean. I keep going over the logo revisions my boss wants and I can’t stop thinking they’re all garbage, even though I’ve already changed them three times. I hate that I get stuck on details no one else will notice, but it’s like I can’t help myself. My roommate keeps texting me about splitting chores tomorrow and I just want everyone to leave me alone for one night. The hum from the fridge is actually louder than I remember, or maybe I’m just more on edge than usual. The deadline’s tomorrow and I’m not even sure the client will like anything I send. I keep telling myself to just finish and sleep, but my brain won’t shut up. I wish I could just hit pause on everything for a few hours. At least the city’s quiet for once.

Had to redo the simulation for the third time today. The code still throws a weird error that I can’t trace, and I’m starting to wonder if it’s something basic I’m missing or just a bug in the library. I’ve been pacing between my laptop and the window, trying to shake off this jittery feeling. The living room feels smaller when I’m frustrated. Sunlight hit the corner of the couch around three, and I caught myself just staring at the dust motes instead of working. Kept telling myself to focus, but my mind keeps jumping ahead to tomorrow’s standup and what questions might come up. I know my work is solid most days, but right now every little setback feels bigger than it is. Maybe I should get some air, but I keep thinking I’ll lose momentum if I step away. My phone buzzed twice this afternoon—ignored both. It’s quiet except for the faint hum from the fridge. Thought about calling someone, but honestly, not sure what I’d even say. I’ll probably go back to the code in a bit, but for now I just needed a break from staring at the screen. Routine is comfortable, but it can also be a trap. Not sure what would actually make me feel better right now. Maybe just need the day to end.

The streetlights flicker above me while I walk, hands deep in my jacket pockets. It’s pretty quiet except for my footsteps and the distant hum of a car radio. The air feels damp tonight, like it might rain, and I keep hearing the sound of my own breathing louder than usual.

Mom’s been on my mind most of the day. Can’t shake the feeling that I should be doing more for her, even though I know there’s not much left I can fix. Being a mechanic makes me think I can repair anything, but I know I can’t fix this. Sometimes I wish I could just work on engines and not think, but tonight everything follows me.

Money’s tight again. Got three jobs lined up for next week, but nothing guaranteed. I worry about bills, then feel guilty for thinking about money when someone I love is hurting worse. I keep telling myself things will even out, but it’s hard to believe that tonight. I hope a better mood finds me in the morning.

The glow from my phone is the only light in the room, and my hands are kind of shaky from scrolling through my bank app too many times. It’s almost 2am, and I know I should try to sleep, but my brain is stuck on the list of things I need to do tomorrow—well, technically today. I have to call the phone company, follow up with two clients for freelance gigs, and see if I can pick up extra hours at the store. The stack of receipts on my desk is ridiculous, like some weird paper monument to how disorganized I’ve gotten lately.

Maybe it wouldn’t feel so heavy if I hadn’t argued with Eli earlier about money and plans and everything we haven’t figured out yet. It just seems like we’re on totally different pages, and I don’t know how to fix it or if it even can be fixed. I keep telling myself things will work out, but sometimes hopeful feels more like desperate. I wish I could just pause everything for a second—just enough time to breathe and not feel like I’m drowning in errands and expectations. I really need to get some sleep before my alarm goes off, but shutting my brain down is not happening tonight.

Just put my phone down after another awkward conversation with Mark about the bathroom schedule. I tried to be diplomatic, but I could feel my voice getting tight when he mentioned how long my showers have been lately. The living room feels quieter than usual, the ticking wall clock suddenly really noticeable. I keep telling myself that sharing an apartment at my age is temporary, just a necessary step while freelancing is so unpredictable. Still, these little moments of social friction wear me out. I wish I could relax in my own space without worrying if I’m stepping on someone else’s toes, literally or otherwise. The sun’s starting to set, the orange light making the room look kind of cozy, which helps me feel a bit more grounded. I know Mark’s not trying to make things tense, and honestly, I appreciate how he tries to talk about issues instead of bottling them up. But sometimes I replay these conversations in my head, worrying if I sounded defensive or inconsiderate. Deep breathing helps, and I keep reminding myself that we’re both doing our best. Maybe once schedules settle down, things will smooth out on their own.

This morning, I remember staring at my phone for almost an hour, flipping between email, my project management app, and the news, trying to will some new work to appear. Even as I was making oatmeal, my mind kept running through the list of invoices still unpaid. Now, after dinner, I’m at the table, dishes pushed to the side, and my laptop open. There’s this odd stillness in the house, but inside my head it feels like a race—like I’m darting from idea to idea, chasing the next project lead.

My focus tonight is sharper than usual, almost like a physical tension in my jaw and shoulders. I spent the last two hours deep-diving into a proposal for a potential client, tweaking every sentence, and researching their company culture to make it perfect. It’s weird how I can get lost in this zone, forgetting how hungry or tired I am until I stop. I know the uncertainty of freelancing is wearing, especially with bills coming up and no guarantee that this pitch will even get a response. Still, I can’t help but feel hopeful. Each time I send something out, I imagine it’s the one that changes everything. The pressure is real, but so is the possibility. I keep telling myself that if I just push a little harder, focus a little more, something good will land. For now, I’m going to try to let my mind slow down and maybe watch a dumb show before bed. One step at a time, I guess.

The afternoon sun is glinting off the windshields around me, and I can hear the distant hum of leaf blowers somewhere behind the lot. I’m wedged into my usual spot, trying to gather my thoughts before heading inside, but my brain feels thick, like wading through fog. Today was supposed to be a bit lighter—at least that’s what I told myself when I checked my schedule this morning—but instead, I’ve been pinging between meetings, client calls, and a hundred Slack messages. My phone keeps buzzing with reminders about groceries, bills, and who’s picking up what for dinner, as if I could forget any of it for a single minute.

I’m grateful my roommate and I can laugh about the chaos of our overlapping calendars, even if it means comparing Google sheets at midnight just to make sure we’re not double-booking the laundry machine. I keep thinking I’ll find a better rhythm, but instead it’s more like juggling eggs while walking on a balance beam—nerve-wracking, but weirdly hopeful. Despite the haze in my head, I’m actually looking forward to one of my projects later; the client finally gave me creative freedom, and that feels rare lately. Just need to remember to breathe and not let the logistics swallow up the good parts. Maybe I’ll hang out in the car for a few more minutes before facing the next wave.

Just closed another job application tab after midnight, and my fingers are still twitching from typing out the same answers for the hundredth time. The glow from my laptop is the only light in the room, and I can hear my brother’s TV through the wall, which makes it so hard to keep my thoughts straight. I keep jumping from one job listing to another, bookmarking positions I know I’ll probably never apply for, but I can’t help it. My mind won’t shut off, running through interview questions, worrying if I’ll say something stupid, or if someone in the house will barge in during a Zoom call again. There’s this tightness in my chest tonight—maybe from all the what-ifs piling up. I wish I could focus on just one thing, but every time I try, another worry pops up. Maybe if I just write everything down, I’ll be able to sleep, though I doubt it. Still, the house is finally quiet enough to think, even if my thoughts are a mess.

Earlier today I almost missed a customer call because my phone was buried under a pile of receipts and takeout menus on the kitchen table. I scrambled to find it, tripped over my own shoes, and finally answered with one shoe on and my brain still foggy. That pretty much sums up how things have been lately—messy, behind, and out of sync. Now it’s past midnight, laptop open, tabs everywhere, and I’m trying to get through the last few support tickets before I crash. I can barely keep my eyes open but the emails just keep coming, like they know exactly when I’m about to give up for the night.

Money’s been on my mind nonstop. Last week was okay, but this week the gigs are drying up again, and it’s hard to plan anything when I don’t know what’s coming in. I keep telling myself it’ll even out, but some days that feels like a lie. On top of all that, I think I pissed off Jamie again. We were supposed to talk after my shift but I got caught up in a chat escalation and forgot to text back. He sent a few messages that I haven’t replied to yet, mostly because I don’t know what to say without sounding like I’m making excuses. I wish I was better at balancing all this crap. There’s always this voice in my head reminding me that I could be more organized, more thoughtful, more…something. But I’m just tired. Maybe tomorrow I’ll get my act together. Right now, the only thing I want is sleep.

Closed my laptop at 1:15 AM and just let my head rest on my arms for a minute, feeling the hum of the coffee shop’s fridge and watching the barista wipe down counters. I was the last customer, nursing a cup of peppermint tea because coffee was out of the question if I wanted any chance at sleep. My mind kept circling back to the phone call with Mom earlier—she sounded so small, her voice fragile in a way that made me ache. I wanted to ask more, to fix something, but she just wanted to talk about the weather and the new neighbors. Maybe she’s protecting me, or maybe I’m protecting myself. I keep telling myself I have time to breathe and process but everything feels like it’s stacked on top of me lately: deadlines, group projects, the empty side of my bed when I get home, and the soft click of my roommate’s door closing at night.

I noticed the smell of cinnamon from someone’s pastry lingered long after they left, and it reminded me of baking with Dad when I was little. The ache of missing him comes in waves—sometimes sharp, sometimes just a dull ache in the background. Grief is strange; it makes me more observant, like I’m searching for pieces of him in everyday things. I wiped away tears before leaving so the barista wouldn’t see. Walked home under the streetlights with my backpack heavier than it should be, wishing I could trade a little of my exhaustion for some peace.

journal_text: Saw a sticky note stuck to my lunch bag this morning, the one I forgot to clear off yesterday—it just said "remember," in my own handwriting, which, honestly, is useless unless I specify what I’m supposed to be remembering. I laughed at myself and then forgot about it until now, when I’m finally getting a breath during this lunch break. There’s the hum of the fridge and the ticking clock in the break room, and my brain feels like it’s running on low battery, just kind of idling. I’m supposed to be using this quiet time to catch up on some emails, but instead I keep replaying last night, which ended with me on the couch, half-watching a documentary, and half-texting Sam—if that’s even what we’re doing, I’m not sure. There’s this weird limbo where I want to ask, “So are we doing this or not?” but I don’t want to seem impatient or, worse, desperate. I don’t think he knows what to say either. It’s been a long time since I’ve had to navigate this sort of thing, and I keep forgetting the rules, if there are any. We were supposed to meet up for dinner but he had to reschedule, and I get that work can be chaotic, but I can’t help but wonder if I’m reading too much into it. Feels like managing a project with shifting deadlines and no project plan, which, as an engineer, is both ironic and a little maddening. My coworkers kept popping in and out of my office all morning, needing things urgently, and I’m starting to feel like everyone wants a piece of me but no one is actually interested in how I’m doing. I keep telling myself to be patient, but I’m tired—more tired than I want to admit. The microwave is beeping now, someone’s heating up soup, and I wish I could just pause everything and have five minutes where no one needs anything from me, including myself. Maybe tonight I’ll just turn off my phone and read, but then again, what if he texts? Ridiculous how much I let that influence my mood. Anyway, lunch is almost over, and I’m still not sure what I was supposed to remember, but I guess I’ll find out eventually, or not.
