journal_text: Woke up feeling kind of flat, which is probably better than yesterday. The kitchen is cold and the sun’s barely up, but I’m already bracing myself for another round of awkward conversation with Dad—he’s been snippy lately, or maybe I’m just more on edge than usual. The cereal box was empty except for crumbs, which somehow feels like a metaphor for how much patience I’ve got left right now. I tried to ask him how he was feeling, and he shot back something about me hovering too much. Hard not to take that personally, even though I know he’s frustrated with everything, not just me. I keep telling myself I need to stop overanalyzing every word, but it’s not like I’m wired to just let things slide. The fridge hums like it’s judging me, and I’m staring out the window pretending to care about the neighbor’s dog digging another hole. I know we’ll both calm down eventually, but mornings like this make it feel like I’m swimming upstream with a backpack full of rocks. Kind of wish I could just leave for work and not think about any of this, but here I am, focused on making sure I don’t screw up again today.

Just closed my laptop after trying to balance next week’s client meetings with the school play and dentist appointments—my head feels like a whiteboard full of scribbles. It’s almost 8:30pm, and I can’t stop thinking about that one spreadsheet formula that won’t work, even though I’m supposed to be off the clock. The barista here wiped down the tables with something lemony, which is oddly comforting, but all it does is remind me of chores waiting at home. I need to sync my calendar with Lisa’s again; she texted earlier that there’s a parent-teacher thing on Thursday, but I’m not sure if I logged it. I wonder if the kids notice how distracted I get, shuffling between appointments and emails, probably more than I’d like to admit. I keep replaying that awkward meeting with my boss—did I over-explain things again? Should’ve just kept it short, but I can’t help myself. My coffee went cold a while ago, but I haven’t bothered getting up for another. Maybe I’ll just head home and hope tomorrow’s less of a puzzle. Can’t shake the feeling I’m dropping some ball somewhere, just not sure which one.

persona.life_context: in school, balancing work and classes

journal_text: The TV is on low in the background, but it’s mostly just the hum from the fridge that stands out right now. It’s late, maybe close to midnight, and I’m stretched out on the couch with my laptop open but not actually doing any schoolwork. I should be reading for tomorrow’s class, but my head feels heavy and I can’t focus. Today at work was a mess, like usual. That new guy kept ignoring what I said about how we organize the stock, and when I tried to correct him, he gave me this look—like I was overreacting or something. It pisses me off how people assume I’m just being difficult when I’m actually the one keeping things from falling apart. I don’t really bother trying to explain myself anymore, not at work, not with classmates either. They all have their own little groups and I’m just there, trying to get through the day without snapping. I know I’m not the easiest person to be around, and I’m not looking for friends, but sometimes it would be nice if people just respected what I said instead of brushing me off. My phone buzzed a few times earlier, probably group chat stuff for a class project, but I haven’t checked. Not sure I care enough to reply tonight. I can already feel the tension in my neck and shoulders, like my body’s just tired of holding back all the things I want to say. This balancing act is exhausting. The only good thing right now is the quiet, even if it just reminds me how alone I am most of the time. Maybe I’ll just close my eyes for a bit and pretend I don’t have to get up and do it all over again tomorrow.

I kept thinking about my bank balance last night, couldn’t let it go. I decided to just get out and walk around the block, even though it was almost midnight. The street was pretty empty, just a few parked cars and some guy walking his dog. I kept checking my phone for no reason, just scrolling through my banking app like something might change if I stared at it long enough.

It’s weird, because work has actually been okay lately. Got a couple of overtime shifts, which helps, but then I start worrying about the bills coming up—rent, phone, groceries. I’m tracking every dollar, trying to make sure I’m not wasting anything, but it’s still tight. I stopped under a streetlight and just stood there for a second, feeling the cold and listening to someone’s TV through an open window.

I know I should be grateful I have a job and all, but sometimes it feels like I’m just running in place. I want to get ahead, but every time I think I’m getting there, something else hits. Still, I felt a bit better walking it off, even if my brain wouldn’t quiet down.

By the time I got back, it was close to 1 a.m. I made a note in my phone to check on a cheaper grocery store this week. Feels like all I do is make lists, but whatever, it’s something. I just want to get enough ahead that I don’t have to think about money every second. Not sure when that’ll happen, but I guess I’ll keep trying.

The low hum of the espresso machine keeps breaking through my thoughts, and the sunlight is catching in the window, making a bright patch on my table. I keep replaying the conversation from last night with him, my mind snagging on every word I chose, every pause. I think I was too blunt, maybe too quick to assume, but I can’t help it when I get anxious about us drifting. The coffee is getting cold while I stare at my phone, waiting for a message that probably won’t come until later. I wish I could just let things go, trust that we’ll figure it out, but I keep obsessing over what I could have said differently. He said I don’t listen, but I’m pretty sure I do—I just get stuck wanting to fix everything immediately. My mother’s voice echoes in my head, telling me to give people space. Ever since she passed, I catch myself wanting to hold on tighter to everyone, afraid of losing more. I’m not sure if that’s making things better or worse. The couple next to me laughs, and I feel separate from it all, like I’m watching people who know how to just be together without analyzing every word. Maybe I need to learn how to do that. I keep writing drafts of a text in my head, but nothing feels right. I wish I knew how to just say ‘I’m sorry’ and let it be enough. The afternoon is slipping by, and I still haven’t figured out what I want to say. At least here, with the noise and the clatter, I don’t have to decide anything yet.

Earlier today, I almost tripped over my youngest’s backpack in the hallway as I was heading out to make breakfast. The house was already humming with voices, and I had to squeeze past my brother who was searching for his keys. Now I’m at my little desk in the corner of my bedroom, where the sunlight is just hitting the edge of my notebook. I tried to catch my breath and gather my thoughts, but the noise from the kitchen drifts in even with the door closed. I keep thinking about what I’m actually doing with my life, and how being a barista sometimes feels like pressing the same button over and over, even though I love the way coffee smells in the morning.

There’s this restlessness inside me lately, like I’m supposed to be building something bigger, but I can’t figure out what it is. I wonder if I’m missing some sign or opportunity just because I’m too caught up in daily routines and not enough in actually looking at myself. My family means a lot to me, but having so little privacy makes it hard to hear my own thoughts for more than a minute at a time. I keep telling myself I’m still young enough to change direction if I want, but then I get pulled back into the next task or someone asks me for help. Maybe later today, I’ll take a walk, even if it’s just around the block. I need to believe things can shift, or at least that I can find some clarity in the middle of all this noise.

Just closed my laptop and left the lights low, headphones still around my neck. Still can't wind down even though it's way past midnight. This afternoon we argued again, something stupid about whose turn it was to cook, but it got bigger, like always lately. Her voice got sharp, I got defensive, and suddenly we're both frustrated and not really listening. Tried to talk it through after, but it felt like walking in circles. She went for a run, I stared at the living room wall and listened to a podcast but didn't really hear any of it. My chest felt tight for hours. Now it's quiet except for the fridge humming and my phone buzzing every so often with unread messages. I keep thinking I should have just let it go, or found better words, or not raised my voice. I want us to feel close again, not like we're opponents. It's hard to rest when the air feels thick between us. She went to bed early, door half-closed, and I keep replaying everything. I’m tired but my head won’t stop. Maybe tomorrow will be easier.

persona.life_context: in school, balancing work and classes

journal_text:
Feeling heavy tonight, not sad exactly, just a lot swirling in my head after dinner. The kitchen still smells like onions and thyme, and I can hear the dishwasher humming. Classes were rough today, barely kept my eyes open through the afternoon demo, and then straight to work for prep. I keep thinking about Dad lately, especially since the doctor called Mom this morning, her voice all shaky telling me about the new tests. Didn’t know what to say so I just started chopping carrots like it’d solve something. 

I’m behind on an assignment for nutrition class and I know I should be working on it right now, but all I want to do is zone out and scroll through my phone. My hands are still sticky from peeling garlic, I should shower but I don’t have the energy. Wondering if I’m doing enough for Mom—should I skip a shift and go home this weekend? Feels like I’m always rushing, never actually there for anyone. Missing family dinners more than I want to admit. Don’t know if I’m handling any of this right, but I guess just writing it out helps a little.

The dishes are stacked in the sink, and I can hear the faint hum of the dishwasher running in the background. There’s a sticky spot on the table from where I spilled a bit of salad dressing earlier, but I can’t bring myself to wipe it up just yet—maybe later. Dinner was leftovers, nothing fancy, but somehow I managed to drop my fork twice, which is basically how today felt: just a little clumsy, a little off-balance but still moving along. I kept checking my work emails during dinner, even though I promised myself I’d log off at 6. Remote work blurs everything together, and I find myself mentally reviewing spreadsheets while staring at my forkful of cold chicken. 

I know I got a lot done—numbers reconciled, invoices sent, even a call with a client who kept talking over me—but I never feel like I’m truly “off” anymore. My mind keeps darting from one unfinished task to the next, and by dinner, I’m both wired and worn out. I caught myself snapping at the cat when she jumped on my laptop again, which made me feel guilty. I wish I could compartmentalize better, but boundaries just melt away when your office is also your kitchen table. Still, I noticed I felt sharper today, more focused—maybe because the weather was gray and I didn’t feel like looking out the window every five minutes. Now, I just want to read a chapter of my book and not think about the numbers until tomorrow, but I know I’ll probably check my phone before bed anyway. Some habits stick no matter how much I try to change them.

Pushed my plate away and stared at my phone for a second, calendar open, as if it held answers. Today was just nonstop—messages from Alex about switching pickup days, then a client canceled last minute, which threw my lunch break out the window. I tried to squeeze in a walk but only got as far as the end of the block before the next reminder buzzed. Spilled a little water on my planner and now the ink is smudged everywhere, can’t even read what I wrote for Thursday.

Trying to plan out the next week, but every time I move one thing, three more conflicts pop up. I told myself to breathe, but it’s like my brain is running ten tabs at once. Still, I managed to laugh with Jamie over dinner when she told me about her group project disaster—felt good to just listen and not try to fix.

Not sure if I’m getting better at this co-parenting thing or just more tired. Sometimes I wish I could just say “no” to one request, but then the guilt creeps in. I know I’m doing my best, but it never quite feels like enough.

Now it’s quiet, just the hum from the fridge and the stack of dishes I’m ignoring for a few more minutes. Maybe I’ll tackle them after I write this, or maybe I’ll just scroll for a bit and let my brain relax. The table’s sticky but I don’t even mind tonight.

persona.life_context: in school, balancing work and classes

journal_text:
I couldn’t print out the project requirements for my group assignment because the printer jammed again, which set off a whole chain of minor disasters this afternoon. I still had to finish debugging a feature for work before my evening class, and the code review comments kept piling up on Slack. I kept switching between tabs, trying to keep track of which window was for school and which was for work, and my calendar kept pinging. At one point, I realized I hadn’t eaten lunch, just half a granola bar from my backpack, and my stomach was making noises loud enough to break my concentration. The room is a mess—papers everywhere, extension cords all tangled under the desk, and my old mug from yesterday still sitting by the lamp. Somehow, I thought I could handle all this when I signed up for classes again, but every week seems to get more complicated.

Despite feeling overloaded, I still believe I can pull this off, but my mind keeps circling back to everything I could be doing better. I worry that I’m letting things slip at work when I focus on school, or vice versa, and I’m never sure if I’m giving enough to either. I keep telling myself it’s just a phase, but sometimes I wonder if I’m just not organized enough. My desktop (the digital one, not the physical one) is a disaster, and I have three different to-do lists scattered across apps, none of which are up to date. I just want to get through this week without dropping any balls. Maybe tomorrow I’ll get up early and try to get ahead, but tonight I just want to close all these tabs and sit in silence for a bit.

Had to double-check my calendar again this morning. I almost forgot I was covering for another counselor at the last minute tonight, and my regular clients still expect their sessions. The dashboard clock says 7:51 a.m., and I’m sitting in my car in the parking lot, trying to mentally map out how I’m supposed to finish reports, answer a backlog of emails, and still get groceries before everything closes. The air smells faintly like wet asphalt. I noticed I left my umbrella in the apartment again, which is annoying because it’s definitely going to rain later.

I keep thinking about how my roommate and I barely see each other these days, just passing notes about who needs the shower first or who’s got groceries. Schedules are a puzzle that never quite fit. I wish I could stop replaying the day in my head before it’s even started, but I keep running through each appointment, wondering if I’ll have enough time to decompress in between. I need to remind myself to eat something before the evening shift starts, otherwise I’ll just be running on caffeine and adrenaline. I know I should be grateful for work, but sometimes the logistics make everything feel more complicated than it needs to be. The car seat is uncomfortably warm now, and I realize I’ve just been sitting here instead of going inside. Time to get moving.

persona.life_context: caring for a parent, stretched thin

journal_text: The streetlights were buzzing faintly as I walked around the block, pulling my coat tighter even though it was only a little chilly. I kept looking at the cracks in the sidewalk, trying to focus on each step so my brain wouldn’t spiral out. It was almost midnight, and I could still see the kitchen light on in our window—Mom probably still awake, maybe waiting for me to come back in. I felt like I should have been studying, but I just couldn’t sit still anymore. There’s this constant feeling like I’m always running late for something, even when I’m not sure what it is. Am I even good at being a student anymore? Or a good daughter? Sometimes it feels like neither, just a mess who keeps forgetting things and letting people down. I tried to take a deep breath and count the cars passing, but that only made me realize how tense my shoulders were. My phone buzzed with another reminder for an assignment due next week and I almost laughed—like that task even matters when Mom needs help with the stairs. I thought about just walking until I felt normal again, but I knew I had to go back inside. Maybe tomorrow will feel less heavy, but I’m not counting on it.

Why does it always feel like one tiny comment can just spiral into this whole thing? Dinner was good tonight, I guess, but I could tell there was tension as soon as we sat down. I tried to talk about the project I’ve been working on, but it was like my words kept getting tangled and I wasn’t really saying what I meant. She kept looking at her phone, which made me feel like I was boring or just too much, but when I asked if something was wrong, she just said she was tired. I know I overthink everything, but it’s hard not to when the air feels so thick. The kitchen light was flickering, which only made me more distracted. I want to be better at this—actually listening, actually saying what’s in my head, but it’s like my thoughts are all jumbled up and I can’t make them line up. I have this hope that tomorrow will be different, that I’ll come up with the right words, but right now my brain’s buzzing and it’s hard not to just retreat. Maybe I just need to write it all out, even if it feels like rambling. I love her, and I want to make this work, but when nights feel like this, I question if I’m just fundamentally missing some key ingredient to good communication. Maybe we’re both just tired. Maybe I just need to breathe and try again tomorrow.

The car insurance renewal forms were buried under a pile of school permission slips and utility bills tonight, and it took me almost half an hour to find them. I was sitting at my desk, the house mostly dark except for my little lamp, trying to sort through paperwork without waking anyone up. The hum of the old computer was louder than usual, probably because it was so quiet. I kept thinking about the argument earlier—how tense things felt at dinner when I brought up the summer schedule. No one wanted to talk about it, least of all me, but I couldn’t just pretend it’ll sort itself out.

I wish I had more space to breathe, or at least a door that locked. Even now I can hear someone moving around in the hallway, probably needing something, and it makes it hard to focus on what I need to do. I ended up just stuffing half the papers into a drawer and telling myself I’d deal with it tomorrow. I know that isn’t the best solution, but right now I just want five minutes of quiet before sleep.

persona.life_context: new city, still building a social circle

journal_text:
Just finished scrubbing down the kitchen and collapsed at the table with a lukewarm glass of water. My feet still ache from the dinner rush, but my mind is buzzing louder than the dishwasher. The new menu items went over well, and a couple of regulars actually complimented the plating, which gave me a little jolt of satisfaction. Still, I keep replaying that moment when I snapped at one of the line cooks for burning the risotto. Was I too harsh? Maybe I could have handled that differently, but it’s hard to switch gears in the middle of chaos.

It’s so strange being in a new city where I know barely anyone outside of the restaurant. Everyone else seems to have their own circles already, and I worry I come off as intense or closed off. Sometimes I wonder if I’m overthinking every small conversation or if I really am making things awkward. I want to be more relaxed, but I can’t help analyzing each interaction, especially when I’m tired. Maybe tomorrow I’ll try to invite someone for a drink after work, even if it feels risky. For now, I just want five minutes of quiet before I drag myself to bed and do this all again.

persona.life_context: new relationship, unsure where it is going

journal_text:
Feeling a little shut down tonight. The air was cold when I walked around the block, and I kept thinking about that awkward pause in our conversation at dinner. I replayed it a few times in my head—did I say something off, or is it just that we don’t know each other that well yet? I’m honestly not sure if I’m being too careful or not careful enough. The streetlights were flickering and there was this old newspaper stuck under a car tire that I couldn’t stop staring at while I tried to collect my thoughts.

I keep telling myself to just breathe and let things unfold, but I’m finding it hard to relax into this new relationship. I like them a lot, but sometimes I worry I’m reading too much into every little thing. My phone buzzed twice in my pocket but I didn’t check it, kind of hoping it was them, kind of hoping it wasn’t. I know I need to let go of trying to plan everything, but it’s hard when I’m used to organizing every detail, even in my own head. I wish I could just enjoy what’s happening without second-guessing every step.

persona.life_context: new relationship, unsure where it is going

journal_text:
Earlier today, I was on the phone with Mom for almost half an hour, listening to her talk about Dad’s latest doctor visit. I kept zoning out, staring at the wilted plant on my window sill, and thinking about whether I should visit home this weekend or just send another text. Now, after dinner, the kitchen still smells vaguely of garlic, and I can hear my roommate laughing at some show in the other room.

I keep thinking about how everyone expects me to be more supportive with Dad’s health stuff, but I honestly don’t know what to do or say. It all feels awkward and forced, and I worry that anything I do will just come across as performative. I tried to read some articles about dealing with family illness, but none of it seemed particularly useful or realistic. Mostly it just made me feel like I’m letting everyone down.

On top of all that, I can’t stop overanalyzing my relationship. He texted me an hour ago, and I keep replaying what he wrote, wondering if I’m reading too much into it or not enough. It’s like my mind is constantly jumping between worrying about my parents, doubting myself, and questioning where this relationship is even heading. I’m tired, but I know if I go to bed now, I’ll just lie awake thinking about all of it.

persona.life_context: new relationship, unsure where it is going

journal_text: Feeling kind of blank tonight, not sad or happy, just this low hum of uncertainty in my head. The lamp’s got that yellow light that makes everything look slightly sick, and my laptop is open but I’m not working—just scrolling, half-reading some article I can’t remember the title of. The clock says 12:41am. I keep thinking about my relationship with Mark (ugh, is it too soon to define it as "relationship"? I don’t even know if he’s thinking about it that way). He texted me earlier but I waited an hour to respond because I didn’t know what to say. Sometimes I wish I were one of those carefree people who just go with the flow, but instead I’m picking apart every word, every silence. It’s exhausting. I want to ask him where he sees this going but then I worry I’ll seem too intense or, I don’t know, needy? The irony is I’m not even sure what I want out of this yet. I’m supposed to be focusing on my thesis anyway, which is laughable because my brain feels like it’s moving through molasses. There’s a half-eaten bag of chips on the table next to my notes, and I keep glancing at both as if one will give me answers. Maybe I’m overthinking, or maybe that’s just my default setting. I keep telling myself I have time to figure things out, but I’m 38 and isn’t that supposed to mean something? Or maybe it means nothing and that’s the whole joke. Anyway, I’ll probably read another pointless thread online before bed and wake up tired, again. At least the cat’s curled up next to me, purring like she’s got it all figured out. I envy that sometimes.

Stepped outside this morning before the kids woke up, just to breathe and move. The air was cool but not cold, and the sidewalk still held a bit of last night’s drizzle. I tried to focus on my steps, on the sound of my shoes against the concrete, instead of the list running through my head. Interview next week, need to check if the calendar matches with the kids’ schedule—already feeling anxious about juggling both. My phone buzzed with a reminder about a parent-teacher call, and I almost turned around, but I kept walking, hands deep in my jacket pockets.

It feels like I’m always double-checking, making sure I don’t miss anything important for them or for me. I wonder sometimes if I’m doing enough, being enough. The uncertainty about work is heavy. Still, I keep telling myself things will shift eventually, that I’ll find something stable. The gentleness I try to show the kids is something I want for myself, too, but it’s hard. Today, at least for a few blocks, I could breathe a little easier.

persona.life_context: caring for a parent, stretched thin

journal_text: My laptop fan is humming louder than usual, almost drowning out the faint sounds of the TV from the living room. I have a stack of printed articles to my left and a mug with the last inch of cold tea to my right, both ignored for the past hour. It’s already dark outside, and I can see my reflection in the window—hair messy, eyes tired. Mom called me twice while I was trying to summarize some research notes, asking if I knew where her slippers were. I found them by the bathroom door. I keep thinking about all the tasks I left half-finished today: emails half-written, dishes soaking, laundry still damp in the machine. Despite that, it felt good to have a productive meeting with Dr. Liu this afternoon, even if I was distracted by my phone buzzing with reminders to order groceries. I wish I could focus longer, but my mind keeps jumping from work to home and back again. I know I’m lucky to have work that matters and to be able to help Mom, but sometimes it feels like I’m never doing enough for either. The desk lamp is making a warm pool of light and I’m trying to let it calm me down. Maybe I’ll read another article before bed, or maybe I’ll just close the laptop and listen to some music instead. It’s hard to tell what will help tonight.

I spent way too long today trying to get my old laptop to recognize the university Wi-Fi, which meant I was late finishing a freelance article that’s been hanging over me for days. It’s a weird feeling, sitting in the car this evening with my backpack on the passenger seat and a bunch of student essays stuffed into a folder, trying to mentally gear up for the night. The parking lot lights are buzzing overhead and the dashboard clock says 7:18pm, and I still feel like I haven’t done enough. My advisor sent another round of comments on my thesis chapter, and every time I look at that email, I freeze up. I know I need to be patient with myself, but it’s so hard when my income is unpredictable and I can’t even plan more than a week ahead. It all piles up—grading, research, invoices that haven’t been paid yet, and my own coursework. I try to remind myself that I’ve managed harder days before, and that I can get through this too, but tonight the overwhelm feels heavy. My mind keeps flitting from one unfinished task to another, and I can’t seem to settle on what actually needs my attention first. The gentle approach I try to take with students feels hard to apply to myself. Maybe I just need to get home, make some tea, and let myself breathe for a bit before I tackle another round of edits. I’m worried about the rent this month, but for now, I just want to focus on getting through tonight.

Feeling all over the place this morning. The kitchen's already humming—fridge humming, the tap drips, my roommate's blender making a racket at 6:10, and I'm trying not to snap. My prep list for tonight is crumpled in my apron pocket, and I keep adding to it every time I remember something else we forgot at the market. Not sure how we're going to both get ready for our shifts—he needs the stovetop for meal prep, but that's my only counter space for pastry dough. I keep telling myself patience, patience, patience, but when the oven timer beeps and then the phone rings, I just want to walk out for ten minutes, breathe, and come back. 

There's been more tension between us lately, mostly because we're both running on little sleep and a lot of stress, bouncing off each other like hot pans on metal racks. I tried to lighten things up by leaving him a dumb sticky note on the fridge last night ("Don't burn the oatmeal again, please"), but not sure it landed the way I hoped. Tonight's schedule looks like a maze—he's out late, I'm home early, and we both need the kitchen at opposite times. I want to keep things warm between us, not just in the oven. Maybe I'll pick up some fresh bread on my break, leave it out with butter, see if a small gesture helps. Restless energy in my chest, but I'm still hopeful we can figure it out.

Just rinsed my plate and left it on the rack, probably should have washed the mug too but I’ll get to it tomorrow, maybe. The kitchen light feels too bright right now, makes the papers on the table look even more chaotic. Spent the whole day trying to get that pitch deck together, but my head keeps bouncing from one thing to the next—slide five, then checking emails, then suddenly wondering if I ever paid the water bill. I keep telling myself the pitch is basically there, just needs a little finessing, but then I look at it and think, well, it’s not exactly what I pictured. I wrote down a list of things to fix and immediately lost the list, so now it’s just a game of trying to remember what was even on it. If I’m being honest, I’m nervous for the meeting next week. Most days I’m convinced I’m onto something, but then I’ll stare at the numbers and get that twisty feeling in my stomach, like I’m forgetting something critical. The clock on the oven says 7:45—I should probably get up and walk it off, but the chair is comfortable and there’s still a bit of wine left. I keep seeing advice about founders needing to meditate or run marathons or whatever, but honestly, I’m just trying not to lose my keys these days. Maybe I’ll get a surge of energy later and finish the deck, or maybe I’ll just watch half an episode of something and call it productivity. I need to remember to email the accountant, too, but every time I open the draft I get distracted by unread Slack messages. Why are there so many updates, and why do I keep thinking I’ll feel ‘caught up’ if I just answer one more? Anyway, at least dinner was decent—leftover pasta, didn’t burn it this time. I’ll probably feel better after a walk, if I ever get up. For now, just going to sit here and hope tomorrow’s brain is a little more organized than today’s.

The air felt heavy on my skin as I walked around the block tonight—humidity clinging even though the sun was long gone. Streetlights threw yellow patches on the sidewalk, and my sneakers scuffed against a stray branch someone hadn’t picked up. I was more focused on my breathing than on the houses passing by, trying to clear my head after the argument with Sarah over dinner.

We never seem to fight about anything big, but somehow the little things pile up. She said I wasn’t listening again, and I wanted to argue back, but honestly, I was just tired. I know I should try harder, put my phone down, look her in the eye, but after a day of meetings and troubleshooting issues at work, my brain feels half-melted. It’s not that I don’t care. I do, probably more than I say. I just get stuck on practicalities and forget to say how I feel.

By the time I rounded the corner and could see our porch light, I’d made up my mind to apologize. I’m not sure if it’ll come out right, but I’ll try to tell her that being tired isn’t an excuse, just where I’m at. I want us to get this right, even if I don’t always know how.

Just put my laptop bag on the passenger seat and stared at the dashboard clock for a minute. Last night ran late—reading articles for the seminar and then chasing down some missing forms for the department. I kept checking my phone, thinking there was another email I’d missed. The car felt cold even with the engine off, and I was too wired to sleep until well after midnight.

Working from home turns into a mess—no clear start or end. Now, sitting here in the parking lot, it isn’t clear whether I’m coming or going. I’ve got two meetings in a row, then a call with my advisor, and after that the day blurs into grading and more reading. I scribbled a list on a receipt last night, but I can’t remember if I packed everything I need. There’s a stack of books in the backseat that I meant to return to the library, and my mind keeps jumping between tasks before any of them are done.

I keep telling myself I’ll get ahead, but every day it feels like I’m barely breaking even. I’m supposed to be learning and growing, but some days the pressure makes the learning feel secondary. Still, I caught myself hoping that the next week will be better organized. Maybe if I can just get through today with no surprises, I can carve out a few hours for actual research. For now, I just need to take a breath and go inside.

Feeling pretty drained right now. I’m on my lunch break, eating a cold sandwich at the kitchen table and trying not to scroll endlessly through job postings. It’s weird how even looking at those listings makes my heart race a little, or maybe that’s just the third cup of lukewarm tea kicking in. Every description sounds like a trap, honestly, with their 'fast-paced environment' and 'must be a self-starter' lines. I can almost hear them laughing as they write it. 

My partner texted to check in, which I appreciate, but it’s hard not to feel snippy when I’m this tired and on edge. We keep talking about communicating better, but some days it feels like we’re just sending smoke signals through a hurricane. Tonight, we’re supposed to have a real conversation about our plans—whatever that means. Part of me wants to just order takeout, put on a dumb show, and ignore the looming pile of adult decisions. 

I know I need to keep pushing, but today it all feels heavier than usual. Maybe I’ll just finish this bland sandwich and go for a quick walk before the next round of applications. At least outside, I can pretend I’m just someone taking a stroll, not someone desperately trying to get her life together.

persona.life_context: in school, balancing work and classes

journal_text:
The hum of the dishwasher is louder than I expected tonight, and the overhead light is a little too bright on the kitchen table. I finished eating about twenty minutes ago, but I haven’t managed to clear my plate yet because my mind is spinning with everything I need to do. This morning started with a missed alarm, which meant I was rushing to get ready before my first online class. I kept thinking I’d get ahead by multitasking—answering Slack messages while skimming reading assignments—but all it did was split my attention. I can’t help but question whether I’m actually absorbing anything in either area.

Balancing work deadlines and assignments is getting trickier, especially with group projects piling up. I made a quick checklist after lunch, but the list seems to grow faster than I can cross things off. My phone buzzed constantly with meeting reminders and emails, which made it hard to focus on the coding problem I was supposed to solve by noon. I know I tend to overanalyze everything, but it feels like if I don’t, something important will slip through. Maybe if I set stricter boundaries for when I check work stuff versus schoolwork, things would feel less chaotic. For now, I just want to get through this week without dropping any balls.

persona.life_context: new city, still building a social circle

journal_text:
Zipped my jacket up as I stepped onto the bus, fumbling with my headphones and nearly dropping my phone yet again. The day dragged on way longer than it should have, mostly because I had to cover for someone who didn’t show up, so I barely got to eat lunch and my feet still hurt. I keep thinking I should get better at planning meals and maybe prepping snacks, but every time I try to start, it just feels so overwhelming—like, where do I even find the energy? The bus is packed and smells like wet sneakers, and I keep bumping elbows with the guy next to me who’s watching some loud TikTok without headphones. Classic.

I’m annoyed at myself for not looking up a better route home or just taking a rideshare, but I’m trying to save money, especially since moving here is costing more than I expected. My new apartment is still half in boxes, and I can’t find my favorite mug, so every morning feels off. I was going to text one of the girls from work to see if she wanted to hang out later, but I chickened out—what if she thinks I’m too much or just awkward? I keep telling myself it’ll get easier, but tonight I just want to get home, eat whatever random food I have left, and maybe zone out to some dumb reality show. Maybe tomorrow I’ll figure out groceries and actually talk to someone new. For now, I’m just tired.

The fridge hums a little louder than usual, and the afternoon sun is slanting through the blinds, making weird stripes on the kitchen counter. Lunch break, but it doesn’t feel like much of a break. I just microwaved leftovers and scrolled through emails with one hand while eating. My tablet is sitting open next to the sink, mocking me with half-finished sketches and a long to-do list. Sometimes it feels like the days just blur together, each one packed with video calls, client edits, and messages that need replies right away.

I thought working remotely would give me more space to breathe, but lately it’s just meant the boundaries are gone. I’m trying to focus on the positives—at least I don’t have a commute, and I can wear paint-stained sweatpants all day if I want. Still, I can’t shake this tired, restless feeling, like I’m never fully caught up. Maybe I’m just being hard on myself, but I need to figure out a better system before I burn out. For now, I’ll just finish this cold rice and hope inspiration hits before my next call.

Dinner was leftovers again, some rice and the last two eggs. I kept counting up what’s left in the fridge, trying to make it last until I get some money in. The table is a mess of receipts and my old phone, calculator open. I keep telling myself it’s temporary, but I don’t know how long temporary is supposed to feel.

After eating, I sat there with the dirty plate, not wanting to move. My mind kept running circles about what I’m doing with my life. There’s this pressure to figure things out, to be more, or at least do something. But nothing feels right or possible right now. I checked job boards again tonight, but everything either wants experience or pays nothing. Sometimes it feels like I’m invisible. I wish I could just stop thinking for a while, but it’s like my head won’t let me. Maybe tomorrow will be clearer, but that feels like a lie I tell myself every night.

The sound of a distant lawnmower blends with the crunch of gravel under my shoes as I loop around the block this afternoon. Sunlight keeps flickering through the tree leaves, making it hard to decide whether I need my sunglasses or not. I keep checking my phone for emails—nothing new, just a reminder about an invoice I sent out last week. It’s always like this, waiting for replies, wondering if I’ll have enough to pay rent and get those new brushes I’ve been eyeing.

My mind drifts between the projects I’ve promised to finish and the ones I want to start for myself. There’s a sketchbook in my backpack that’s been sitting untouched for days, which makes me feel guilty, like I’m slacking even though I know I’ve been hustling nonstop. The to-do list in my notes app is longer than it should be, but at least it’s organized—deadlines, client names, rough ideas. I wish I could turn off the part of myself that always feels like I’m falling behind, but maybe that’s what keeps me moving.

The mail truck passes by, and I wonder if there’s anything for me today—probably just bills. My headphones are half on, half off, because I want to hear the world but also zone out. I’m calm, but underneath there’s this steady pressure to make sure nothing slips through the cracks. I tell myself to just focus on what I can control: finish one piece at a time, answer those emails tonight, maybe reward myself with a walk like this more often. For now, I just keep moving, counting the steps to the next corner.

Feeling kind of tense this afternoon, not sure exactly how to shake it off. The bedroom desk is covered in the usual mess: post-it notes with reminders, my planner open to the week, a mug with cold tea I forgot about. I keep glancing at my phone, waiting to hear back from him about the pickup time for Ava. It’s always a negotiation, never smooth, because his schedule is all over the place and then I have to scramble to change mine. I wish I could just let things slide but I keep thinking if I was more organized, or if I could just anticipate his weird last-minute changes, then maybe Ava wouldn’t have to be shuffled around so much. It’s probably not even a big deal in the long run but it feels like a failure every single time something doesn’t line up. I keep replaying our texts in my head, analyzing if I sounded annoyed or if I should have just agreed right away instead of asking questions, but I can’t help but want some clarity. Part of me wants to just say yes to everything and be easygoing, but the other part is tired of always being the one who adjusts. Sometimes I wonder if I’m making it harder than it has to be, or if I’m just kind of stuck in this pattern of trying to control things that are basically impossible to control. The sunlight through the window is making the dust in here really obvious and I’m noticing every little thing that’s out of place, which is probably not helping. I guess I’m hyperfocused and it’s making me pick apart all the small stuff, like if I had just left work on time or if I had prepped dinner earlier, then maybe the evening wouldn’t be so rushed. I know I’m being self-critical but it’s hard to stop, especially when there’s this constant pressure to make life smooth for Ava. My mind just keeps looping through the schedule, the handoffs, the little frictions, wondering if it’ll ever feel easy. Maybe I just need to step back and let some things go, but that feels so much easier said than done. Wish I could just hit pause for a bit and breathe without thinking about the next thing I might be forgetting.

Just tapped my bus card and found an empty seat by the window. This morning felt like a blur—got up late, barely had time to grab a granola bar before rushing out. I keep thinking about how I need to log every cent spent lately; even the $2 for this bus ride feels significant when I’m watching my bank balance dwindle. Work was nonstop—people everywhere, credit card machines beeping, and managers hovering more than usual. I sold some overpriced headphones to a guy who didn’t seem convinced, but hey, that’s the job. My mind keeps jumping around: what groceries I still need, whether I should cancel my streaming subscription, if I’ll have enough for rent. It’s hard to focus on one thing for long, but at least I felt somewhat productive today, even if I’m not sure it matters. The lights on the bus flicker a bit as we hit a pothole. Someone spilled coffee across the aisle and it smells weirdly sweet, mixing with the rain on the windows. I keep checking my phone, half-expecting some good news, but nothing so far. Part of me is restless, wanting more out of this routine, but mostly I’m just relieved to be heading home.

This afternoon, I caught myself staring out the window during my free period, watching the wind mess with the flag on the playground. I should have been grading, but my mind kept drifting to the stack of lesson plans still waiting for me. Now it's past 11 PM, and I'm finally home, sitting at the kitchen table with my planner and a cup of herbal tea. The house is quiet except for the hum of the fridge, which is oddly comforting. I logged every grocery and supply expense into my spreadsheet, feeling both proud and slightly anxious at how quickly the numbers add up. I wish I didn't have to think about money so much, but these days every little purchase feels like a decision. Teaching used to feel more straightforward; now there's a constant pressure to do more with less, and I can't help but worry about how stretched things are getting at school too. I noticed a few students seemed unusually withdrawn today, but there wasn't time to check in with them properly. The to-do list never ends, and I keep wondering if I'm missing something important while trying to keep everything together. Still, I feel calm right now, maybe just tired enough that the worries have quieted down for the night. I hope tomorrow feels a little lighter.

Just finished scrolling through some tech news on my phone, trying to shake off that weird heaviness that settles in when the house is too quiet. It’s still early, so everyone else is either asleep or pretending to be, and I have the living room to myself. I keep thinking about how different mornings used to feel when grandma was around—her voice echoing from the kitchen, the smell of ginger tea wafting in. Now, there’s just this emptiness mixed with the hum of the fridge and the soft ticking of the wall clock. I tell myself I’m handling her passing well, but sometimes I catch myself looking for her slippers under the coffee table or expecting her to ask for help with her tablet. Maybe I’m being too hard on myself for not moving on faster, but it feels like life keeps piling on small reminders when I least expect them. My family doesn’t talk much about her, and maybe that’s why I feel restless, like I should be doing something more or being stronger for everyone. At least work keeps me occupied—debugging a new module today, which should be a good distraction. Still, I wish there was more space for privacy around here, somewhere I could just process things without worrying about someone overhearing. For now, I’ll just hang out on this couch, try to focus on the things I can control, and remind myself that missing her is okay. Maybe that’s what moving forward looks like, even if it’s messy.

Steam curls up from my mug, and the hum of the espresso machine is almost loud enough to drown out my phone’s constant buzzing. The table here is sticky, and I keep losing focus, jerking back to the laptop screen whenever a new message pops up from work. It’s barely 9:30 and I already feel like I’m running behind, but everyone on the team wants answers instantly. I said yes to covering someone else’s shift out of habit, even though my own list is a mess. I wish I was better at saying no, or at least not so reactive when someone asks for help. The barista called my name wrong again, but I just smiled, too tired to correct him. I can’t decide if it’s better to hide in public like this or just stay home where the boundaries blur even more. Maybe I’ll order another croissant before the lunch rush starts, just to buy myself a few more minutes away from the screen.
