journal_text:
This morning I dropped my wrench under the truck and for a second I just stared at it, thinking about how things used to be easier in the old shop. Funny how something small like that can set you off. Now it's afternoon, I'm in the parking lot, trying to get my head straight before clocking in for the late shift. The sun's beating down on the dashboard and everything smells like hot rubber and metal. 

Still haven't made any real friends here, just a couple of guys who'll nod at me or talk about the weather. I miss being able to joke around with people who actually know me. But I'm getting by. Work keeps me busy, which is good—there's always something to fix or tune up. I keep telling myself that it'll get easier, that I'll find my people eventually. For now, I just focus on the next engine, the next job, and getting through today without screwing something up. Maybe that's enough for now. Time to head in.

Had to double-check some invoices this morning because my mind kept drifting back to last night. I was up too late, scrolling on my phone, thinking about Mom’s last hospital visit and how quiet the new apartment feels. The kitchen clock ticking was the only sound after midnight. I keep unpacking, but the boxes just remind me of everything I left behind. My brother texted about Dad’s test results—nothing new, but I still felt a pang. Eating my sandwich now, the lettuce is wilted and I barely taste it. I know I need to settle in, but I’m not sure what that even means anymore. Maybe I’ll try to call home later, if I can focus long enough to dial.

This morning I was looking for my keys and found my son's crumpled drawing shoved in the basket by the door. He’s been drawing a lot lately—mostly superheroes with big hands. I stopped, just stood there in the hallway, staring at it longer than I meant to. I thought about how quickly he’s growing up, how I barely notice the changes until something like this hits me out of nowhere. 

Now it’s just after 5pm, and I’m sitting in the car, engine off, outside what used to be my office. I’m early for picking him up—my turn tonight. The parking lot is mostly empty, except for a few cars and some scattered shopping carts. My phone keeps buzzing with calendar reminders, but I ignore them for a minute, trying to gather my thoughts. Coparenting has become a series of negotiations and reminders, always a little tense but manageable. I keep a notebook in the glovebox for schedules, but sometimes it feels like I’m just patching things together day by day. My ex and I messaged earlier about a dentist appointment for next week, and even that felt heavier than it should. I’m focused on making things work, but I miss the routine of a job—something predictable. Grief sneaks in sometimes over things I didn’t expect to miss: work potlucks, the sound of printers, even the crappy coffee. Tonight, though, I’m determined to keep things steady. Maybe we’ll have breakfast for dinner and watch something silly. I want the evening to feel easy, even if coordinating it wasn’t. The sky’s turning a little orange, and the air smells like cut grass. Time to go.

persona.life_context: new city, still building a social circle

journal_text: There’s a half-eaten sandwich next to my laptop and I’m just staring at the blinking cursor because my brain’s basically sludge. Finished my shift around 11pm—still getting used to the weird hours here. Place was slammed, and I caught myself snapping at someone over the mop bucket being in the wrong spot, which I feel bad about now. I keep worrying that I’m not really cut out for this supervisor thing, like I’m missing something everyone else already knows. After work, I walked home because I needed the air, but the city still feels like a bunch of unfamiliar puzzle pieces. I texted James from work to see if he wanted to hang out but he was busy; not sure if it’s just polite brush-offs or if I’m overthinking. I put on some random sitcom to fill the noise but it mostly just made me notice how quiet the apartment is. I keep telling myself it’ll get easier, that I’ll find my crowd, but tonight it feels like I’m just drifting. Maybe I’m being dramatic—other people have done this before. I guess I just miss having people who get my dumb jokes or know when I’m being sarcastic. My phone keeps buzzing with work group chat stuff, but I don’t want to deal with it right now. Just want to eat, shower, and go to bed, but I’m too tired to even finish the sandwich. Tomorrow’s another long shift, but maybe I’ll try that trivia night after. Not sure. For now, I’ll just watch the city lights out the window for a bit and hope sleep comes fast.

persona.life_context: caring for a parent, stretched thin

journal_text:
I spent most of the afternoon troubleshooting a bug in the system at work, but I kept getting interrupted by texts from Mom. She needed help finding her medication again, and then she wanted to talk about her next doctor’s appointment. I was trying to focus, but my mind kept jumping between code and her needs. It’s hard to pretend I’m present for my job when I’m so distracted.

My desk is cluttered with sticky notes—work reminders on one side, and doctor schedules on the other. Every time I try to clear a space, something else piles up. I keep telling myself that I just need to get organized, but there’s never enough time to actually do it. I feel pulled in two directions, and I’m not sure how to be enough for either side.

Lately, I’ve been thinking a lot about what I’m actually working toward. Am I just keeping everything afloat, or am I building something meaningful? Some days I feel hopeful, like there’s a point to the effort, but today I just feel tired. Who am I outside of being an engineer and a caregiver?

Maybe that’s why I keep taking on so much—I’m worried that if I stop, I’ll have to face the uncertainty underneath it all. For now, I’ll just try to get through the rest of my task list and hope tomorrow feels a little lighter.

Just got back from walking around the block, mostly to clear my head and try to shake off this heavy tiredness that’s been hanging over me all day. The air was cooler than I expected for June, and I kept my hands jammed in my pockets, just listening to the sound of my own footsteps on the sidewalk. It’s weird, freelancing was supposed to give me more control, but lately it only feels like I’m floating from one project to another, not really sure where it’s going. My phone buzzed twice—probably another email about a deadline, but I ignored it. There’s this strange hollow feeling when the projects end and I’m back to searching for the next, like I keep hitting reset on everything. Saw someone’s porch light flicker and wondered if they’re also awake thinking about money and meaning at 11pm. I keep telling myself that building something for myself is worth the stress, but some nights, like tonight, I just feel like a ghost walking around my own neighborhood, not sure what comes next. Maybe I’m just overtired and making it all worse in my head, but I wish I knew if I’m actually building toward something real, or if I’m just keeping busy to avoid the bigger questions. Even now, as I write this, I’m looking for some kind of sign that I’m on the right path, but there’s only the hum of the fridge and the faint sound of cars on the main road. I need to get some sleep, but my mind won’t quit.

persona.life_context: caring for a parent, stretched thin

journal_text:
There’s a half-finished mug of chamomile tea next to my laptop, and I keep staring at the golden rim, feeling like I should be winding down but my brain is spinning. Tonight was another argument with Mom about her medications—she insists she doesn’t need the new ones, and I’m trying to be patient, but I snapped. I hate that I lose my cool, especially when I know she’s scared and stubborn because she’s losing control over her own life. The guilt hits hard, like a weight that doesn’t lift no matter how many deep breaths I try to take.

The project at work is dragging, too—every email I open feels like a little landmine. I caught myself zoning out in the middle of a Zoom call, thinking about whether I remembered to lock up her prescriptions. My team expects answers, but honestly I’m barely keeping track of who needs what. I keep wondering if I’m missing something obvious that would make all of this easier, but there’s always another problem to pick apart. It’s exhausting to always be the one who has to figure it out, both at home and at work.

I wish I had someone to talk to who really gets it, but every time I try to open up to friends they just tell me I’m strong and I can handle it. That just makes me feel more alone, honestly. The desk lamp is too bright and I should go to sleep, but I’m just not ready to let go of the day, even if it’s been a mess. Maybe tomorrow I’ll apologize to Mom, or maybe I’ll just do better. I don’t even know what doing better looks like anymore.

Feeling a bit dull this morning, like my mind hasn’t quite switched on yet. The kitchen is quiet except for the hum of the fridge and the click of the kettle as it finished boiling. I noticed I was standing there holding a mug for a little too long, lost in thought before I even made the tea. It’s early—barely past 6 a.m.—and my body is moving through the motions, but my head feels wrapped in cotton. I used to enjoy this time of day for its peace, but lately it’s more like a checkpoint before work begins rather than a moment to savor. The tile floor felt cold under my feet and I kept thinking that I should have put on socks, but didn’t bother. The milk was almost out, and I made a mental note to get more on my way home, but I’m not confident I’ll remember later.

I tried to map out my tasks for the shift ahead. There’s a meeting I need to run and a schedule to finalize, and I’m already anticipating the small issues that will pop up—someone calling in sick, or the register acting up again. I’m patient with my team, but I can’t help feeling slightly restless, wanting the day to move forward already. Living alone has its perks, but on mornings like this, I wonder if a little conversation might help clear the fog. I noticed the dish soap bottle is almost empty too. I’m making a lot of small lists in my head but not writing anything down, which I know isn’t ideal. The routine is steady, but some days it feels more like autopilot than intention. The tea didn’t taste quite right, but I drank it anyway. I’m hoping as the morning goes on, my mind will catch up with my body. For now, I’ll just focus on getting out the door on time and let the rest unfold as it will.

The hallway light was still on when I finally looked up from the calendar app, thumb rubbing at a sticky spot on the screen from earlier. It’s almost midnight and the apartment’s gone quiet except for the hum of the fridge and the faint traffic outside. I spent most of the evening going back and forth with Sam’s mom about who’s got pick-up next week, juggling our work shifts and her dentist appointment. There’s a weird comfort in the routine, even though it’s exhausting sometimes. I noticed today that I didn’t feel that old ache in my shoulder—that’s a win, I guess. Grief feels less sharp tonight, more like background noise, which is a relief. I caught myself smiling at the idea of Sam’s science project, even if it means another late night with glue sticks. I know these days are busy, but I’m starting to see small stretches of peace in between the scheduling and the loss. Maybe that’s enough for now.

Felt kind of on edge this afternoon, so I decided to get out and walk around the block, hoping the movement would help settle my thoughts. The sky was overcast and the air smelled faintly of rain, which was strangely comforting. My phone buzzed a few times with Slack messages, but I ignored them for a bit—I just needed a break from the constant pinging. Lately, it feels like my work life and personal life have blurred together so much that there’s no real boundary anymore. As a founder, I know I signed up for a certain level of chaos, but sometimes I wish I could shut it all off, just for an hour or two. I keep thinking about the awkward conversation I had with a team member earlier; I tried to be gentle, but I could sense tension, and now I’m second-guessing everything I said. Maybe I should follow up with her tomorrow, just to make sure we’re okay. It’s hard not to take things personally when everything feels so close. I glanced at some neighbors tending their gardens and felt a pang of envy for people who seem to have clearer lines between work and home. The walk helped a little, but as soon as I got back, the emails and messages were waiting, like they never left. Sometimes I wonder if I’d feel less restless if I could just learn to switch off. For now, I’ll try to remind myself that it’s okay not to have all the answers today.

There’s a stack of dirty plates still sweating on the table, and my hands smell faintly of garlic and dish soap. I keep thinking about the conversation tonight—if you can call awkward silences and passive aggressive suggestions about my "culinary experiments" a conversation. It’s only been a few weeks since I moved here and I already feel like I’m some kind of foreign spice no one knows how to use. The kitchen is the only place I remotely understand, but even there, it’s not my kitchen, just this rental with a stove that runs too hot and cabinets that creak like they’re warning me off. I tried to make something familiar for dinner, but apparently "too much rosemary" is a crime among these people. Someone—maybe Mark?—made a joke about "fancy chef food" and everyone laughed except me. I laughed, technically, but it was more of a dry cough. It’s exhausting, keeping up with this subtle game of who’s normal and who’s just passing through. Every little comment about "how things are done here" feels like a reminder that I’m still an outsider, even after unpacking all my knives and spices. I miss my old crew, the ones who would just grunt their approval or tell me outright if something sucked. Here, it’s all smiles and coded language, and I can’t tell if I’m being accepted or just tolerated. I should probably clean the table but my legs feel like lead pipes and I just want to sit for a minute longer, even if it means staring at the mess. Maybe tomorrow I’ll figure out how to blend in better, or at least pretend I care about bland food and small talk. For now, I’ll just let the plates sit and hope no one comes back in to see me sulking at the remains of dinner.

persona.life_context: new city, still building a social circle

journal_text:
Phone buzzing in my lap, keys still in the ignition, and I’ve managed to spill protein bar crumbs all over the passenger seat again. 7:42 pm, edge of the lot, sun just dipping behind the ugly brick building across the street, and I’m early for once. The windows are fogging a little from my breath—guess I’m more anxious about tonight’s intake session than I thought. New client, new issues, and I’m already running through a dozen scenario trees in my head. I keep thinking about how I don’t actually know anyone well enough here to just call and decompress after work. Funny, I tell people to build support networks all day. Maybe I should write myself a prescription for my own advice.

It’s loud in my head—lots of shoulds and maybes. I keep checking my watch, as if that’ll speed things up. Noticed a weird buzzing sound from the dashboard but can’t decide if it’s something mechanical or just my brain making up problems to fix. I left my lunch tupperware under the seat again; smells like old broccoli. I’m trying to focus on the positives: work is steady, I’m learning the city inch by inch, and the grocery store clerk finally recognized me tonight. Tiny victories, I guess. I’ll go in soon, smile, listen, and maybe by the end of the night I’ll feel like I belong a little more here. For now, just me and the crumbs, waiting for the next thing to happen.

Feeling worn out as the bus rocks back and forth under the streetlights. The day blurred together—work calls overlapping with another round of messages from my sister about Mom’s latest doctor appointment. I tried to focus on a client brief, but my mind kept drifting to the hospital smell, the way Mom’s hands look smaller now. It’s strange how the hum of the bus almost matches the quiet in those waiting rooms.

Remote work was supposed to make things easier, but I think it just made it harder to keep any boundaries. I logged off late again tonight, barely noticed the sun going down. Still, I’m glad I could answer when my nephew called, even if I didn’t have anything helpful to say. I wish I could do more for everyone, but mostly I just listen.

Looking out the window, I can’t tell if I’m more tired from the work or the worry. The city looks the same as always, neon signs and people bundled up against the night. I’ll try to sleep early, but my brain will probably keep turning things over. Maybe I’ll call Mom in the morning, just to hear her voice and remind her I’m here.

The dog’s toy squeaks under my foot as I shift to get comfortable on the couch, sunlight coming in at an angle that hits the side of my laptop. It’s mid-afternoon, maybe close to three, but the day feels vague, stretched out by interruptions. I had four work calls crammed into the morning and barely got through two emails before someone needed lunch, then a glass of water, then help finding the remote. The line between work and caregiving is basically gone—sometimes I’m typing an update for a client while listening for the microwave to beep, or answering a question about insurance forms while my inbox pings nonstop. There’s a constant low-level guilt, like I’m not doing either job well enough, though when I step back, I know I’m giving what I can. The house smells faintly like toast, and there’s a pile of clean laundry I keep ignoring on the armchair. I keep thinking I should take a walk, but it’s easier to just stay put and use the quiet moments to breathe. The laptop battery is almost dead, so I’ll need to move soon, but right now I’m just sitting with the hum of the air purifier and the distant sound of traffic outside. I don’t feel rushed, which is rare, but I know the next request is coming—maybe a snack, maybe a spreadsheet review. I wish there was a clearer boundary between my jobs, or at least a door I could close. Still, I’m hopeful things will settle, or I’ll get better at managing all this. Gentle reminders to myself help: drink water, move my legs, don’t judge the mess so harshly. The day isn’t over yet, and that’s good enough for now.

I felt oddly steady as I rode the bus home late last night, pressed against the cool window, watching streetlights flicker over empty sidewalks. The hum of the engine and the faint scent of rain on the seats gave me a quiet place to think. Lately, I’ve been wondering if I’m still the same person I was before coparenting became my life’s structure, before my calendar was a mess of drop-offs and writing deadlines. Sometimes I miss the me who didn’t have to coordinate everything—who could just disappear into a story for hours and not resurface until I was hungry. Now, it’s all reminders and shared apps, always someone else’s schedule to consider. I do love the warmth of my little family, but I keep asking myself where writing fits, who I am outside the roles I juggle. Maybe I’m just restless, but there’s a kind of comfort in the uncertainty too, like standing at a crossroads and realizing you don’t have to pick a direction yet. Last night, watching my reflection in the dark bus window, I almost recognized myself.

Just closed my laptop after scrolling through job listings for what felt like an eternity. It’s almost 10 pm, the TV is on low in the background, and I’m sprawled out on the couch with my feet half-buried under a throw blanket that never seems to stay on straight. The apartment smells like the takeout we had earlier—leftover curry and maybe a hint of burnt rice from when I tried to “help” in the kitchen. I keep telling myself tomorrow will be the day I finally write a decent cover letter, but tonight, I’m letting that anxiety sit next to me like an overeager dog.

I’m trying to focus on the positive. We actually managed to talk through that stupid argument from last night without either of us raising our voices, which is a small miracle. I made a joke about my "impeccable timing" when I brought up the topic during her favorite show, and she rolled her eyes but smiled, so I’ll take that as progress. Communication isn’t always smooth—sometimes it’s just a series of awkward attempts, but at least we’re both trying. I keep reading that relationships are supposed to be "work," but I think they’re more like ongoing group projects with no clear deadline and a lot of late-night check-ins.

Still, there’s a part of me that feels restless. Not having a job is starting to feel like carrying around an invisible backpack full of rocks. I keep wondering if I’m missing some trick that everyone else seems to know. But then she’ll laugh at something stupid I say, or I’ll catch the cat doing something ridiculous, and for a second, I remember that life isn’t just about productivity. Maybe tomorrow I’ll try again with the applications—or maybe I’ll just make breakfast for both of us and call that a win.

Just closed my laptop after staring at the same spreadsheet for, what, an hour? The numbers are all blurring together and I’m pretty sure I started counting the little marks on my pen at some point. It’s quiet in here except for the hum from the heater and the occasional creak from the hallway. I keep thinking about that email my supervisor sent—nothing bad, just more deadlines I wasn’t ready for. My brain feels like it’s full of cotton, which is not great timing considering all the data I’m supposed to analyze by Thursday.

I was supposed to talk to Jamie about something important tonight but I keep putting it off. Communication, communication, communication—so easy to say, so weirdly hard to do when my head’s like this. There’s a mug with cold tea sitting next to me, and I can’t remember when I made it. Maybe if I just write out what I need to say, it’ll come out better? Or maybe I’ll just forget the point halfway through, classic me. Anyway, I should probably try to get up and stretch or something, but I’ll probably just scroll through my phone for a bit and pretend it counts as a break.

persona.life_context: in school, balancing work and classes

journal_text: The hum of the dishwasher mixes with the low chatter from the TV in the background, half-watched and mostly ignored. It’s late—close to 10:30, I think—and I’m sprawled on the couch with my laptop still open on the coffee table, half-finished spreadsheet sharing space with lecture notes from class earlier. Today felt like a marathon with no finish line. Work emails kept coming in until nearly 7, and I barely managed to log into tonight’s seminar on time. I keep telling myself that this is manageable, just a rough patch, but I’m tired and my mind keeps wandering to everything I might be forgetting. There’s an assignment due in two days that I haven’t even outlined, and I caught a mistake in a project plan this afternoon that I should have caught days ago. Being back in school at this age is a challenge I underestimated. Everyone seems so quick to pick things up, while I have to fight the urge to double-check every detail. Still, there’s a part of me that enjoys the push. I want to prove to myself I can do this, even if it means feeling stretched thin. The house is quiet except for the occasional clink of dishes settling, and I’m grateful for this little pocket of calm. I know I could use the time to get ahead, but tonight I just need to breathe and let my brain slow down for a bit. Maybe tomorrow I’ll wake up with a clear sense of what matters most, but for now, I’m just trying to be okay with where I am.

persona.life_context: in school, balancing work and classes

journal_text:
This morning at work, I got into a stupid argument with a coworker about who was supposed to handle a return. It was honestly pointless but it annoyed me way more than it should have. The rest of my shift just dragged and I kept replaying it in my head, thinking of all the better things I could have said. After work I had to rush straight to class, barely had time to grab a sandwich and my notes were a mess.

Now I’m at my desk, finally able to breathe for a second. My room is a mess, papers everywhere, and my laptop’s fan is way too loud. I’m tired but I know I still have to finish an assignment for tomorrow. Even though today felt rough, I keep telling myself it’ll get better. I just need to push through this week.

The quiet hum of the fridge is louder than usual tonight, and the streetlights throw a faint orange glow onto my desk. I keep glancing at the pile of textbooks, half-tempted to pick one up, but my mind is still stuck on this morning.

Mom’s doctor called early, just as I was about to head to campus. It wasn’t bad news, not exactly, but I could hear the worry in her voice afterward. I tried to reassure her, but it’s hard when I’m not sure I believe myself. It’s moments like these when I wish I could do more, but money is tight and my options feel limited.

I spent most of the day in class, but my focus kept drifting. Every time I thought about the group project or the quiz I need to study for, I’d remember Mom’s face at breakfast — tired, but pretending to be fine for my sake. I know she’s trying to shield me from the worst of it, but I see through it. I always have.

Now it’s almost midnight and I’m tracking the last few dollars in my budget spreadsheet again. I want to be patient with myself and with her, but the pressure is building from all sides. Still, I’m determined to keep going, even if it means moving inch by inch through days like this.

persona.life_context: in school, balancing work and classes

journal_text: Feeling pretty steady at the moment, just waiting in the car before I head into the coworking space. I triple-checked my backpack because I keep having this nagging feeling I forgot my laptop charger again, but nope, it's actually there this time. I have a project deadline this afternoon and then a quiz for my online class tonight—why did I think taking two classes while freelancing would somehow be relaxing? I keep telling myself it’s all temporary, but today it all feels stacked kind of high. The sun is out and there’s a weirdly sweet smell from the bakery a few doors down, which almost makes me want to just walk over and ditch my plans for a croissant, but I know I won’t. Sometimes I wish I could let myself do something totally unplanned and not feel guilty. The calendar on my phone is ridiculous—it’s just wall-to-wall reminders and color-coded chaos, but that’s kind of exciting too, I guess. I like the idea that things could work out even if they’re a mess right now. Maybe after I finish my work and the quiz, I’ll just go for a walk and forget about everything for a little while. It’s funny how calm I feel even though the day looks so packed. I think I’m getting better at riding out these busy spells instead of panicking about them. Anyway, time to go in and see if I can find a good spot near an outlet.

Half-awake, I remembered dropping my phone in the sink while brushing my teeth. Water everywhere, and I just stood there, annoyed but too tired to even curse. Now I’m in the kitchen, standing by the fridge because I can’t find the energy to make breakfast. It’s still dark outside, and the house is quiet except for the hum of the old refrigerator.

I’m thinking about all the emails waiting for me at work. Mondays are always too much. My mom walked in for a minute, said good morning, and then left, probably sensing I wasn’t up for talking. I wish I had my own space, but privacy isn’t really a thing here. I keep checking the clock on the microwave, hoping time will slow down. I feel restless, like I should be doing something important, but my brain isn’t cooperating. There’s a pile of unopened mail on the counter. I keep staring at it, not really seeing anything. Maybe I’ll just grab a banana and leave early. Work is stressful lately and I’m already tired before the day’s even started.

Half a sandwich sits forgotten on my plate, mustard starting to congeal. I keep checking my phone, like maybe he’ll text, but actually I don’t even want to see the latest round of half-apologies. I can’t figure out how to fix this thing between us—maybe that’s why I keep making lists about kitchen storage instead of calling him back.

The office is quiet except for someone’s lunch bag crinkling nearby—how do other people seem so at ease with their lives? My head’s buzzing with all the tasks I still need to wrangle, but all I can think about is our last conversation: him saying I’m distracted, me saying he never listens, us talking in circles until we’re both tired. I wanted moving to be a fresh start, but apparently I packed up all our old arguments and brought them along.

Optimism is supposed to be my thing, but today it feels more like a punchline. I know we’ll talk again (probably tonight), and maybe I’ll manage to be less defensive or at least remember to breathe before I answer. For now, I’m just eating around the crusts and hoping nobody notices I’m not really hungry. Maybe I should just text him first. Or maybe I’ll just finish this sandwich and see how I feel in ten minutes.

Kind of numb this morning, just parked and staring at the dashboard lights. Not sure why everything feels so muffled, like my brain is wrapped in cotton. I keep rubbing my eyes hoping it’ll clear, but it doesn’t. The radio is on low, some talk about weather, but I can’t focus on what they’re saying. I keep thinking about Mom, how she used to call every Tuesday, and now Tuesdays just feel like any other day. I told myself I’d try to focus on schoolwork today, but my head’s just not in it. The pile of assignments on my laptop in the backseat is almost taunting me.

Freelance gigs have been slow this month, and the uncertainty is eating at me. I keep running calculations in my head about rent and groceries, but then I just get distracted by this heavy sadness. The car smells like old takeout and the air is a bit stuffy, but I can’t bring myself to open the window yet. Family keeps texting in the group chat, checking in, but I haven’t replied. I don’t really know what to say. Maybe if I just sit here a few more minutes, things will make more sense. Or maybe they won’t. Either way, I guess I’ll go in soon.

I remember this morning, I had to scramble looking for Anna’s favorite socks before she would even consider getting dressed. The sun was barely out, kitchen light flickering, and I was already running on fumes after being up twice in the night. Made eggs, forgot the toast, she wanted toast. The mental checklist just keeps cycling—meds, breakfast, school bag, water bottle, keys, wallet. I keep telling myself to slow down but then something else pops up, like the nurse’s forms I forgot to sign. On the bus now, finally sitting, my bag feels heavier than it should. My hands are shaky, probably not enough food, and I keep thinking about the way I snapped at Jamie about the laundry—regret hits fast, I hate that. Long-term relationship is supposed to get easier but all these little details trip us up. We talked about trying to listen better, but by 10am I already felt too tired to listen to anyone. The bus is crowded, smells like rain and old upholstery, someone’s music leaking through headphones. I’m grateful for the work I get to do, being there for them, but I wish I didn’t always feel like I’m behind. Sun is coming through the window now, makes things feel a bit softer. I need to apologize tonight, or at least try to talk. Maybe we can figure out how to share the load better, but I don’t even know where to start. Just want everyone to feel okay, including me, even if it’s messy.

Head’s buzzing and I’m tired but not sleepy, more like just overloaded, sitting on the couch after lunch, laptop closed but the charger’s still plugged in—why do I always do that? The TV is on low, some rerun nobody’s really watching, and the house feels extra crowded even though it’s just the usual people. I can’t stop replaying that argument I had with her about the weekend, the way she kept looking away when I was talking, like she was bracing for a fight I didn’t really want to have. It’s like every conversation lately has this edge, like we’re on different tracks or talking over each other, and then later I’ll remember some detail she mentioned days ago that I completely missed in the moment. Feels like I can’t focus on anything for more than five seconds, maybe too much going on with my studies but also this constant background tension at home, so even when I try to zone out, I catch myself scanning for signs—tone of voice, footsteps, doors closing a little too hard. 

It’s so hard to talk in this house without someone else overhearing, and every time I try to bring something up, there’s always a sibling or a parent walking by or asking what’s for dinner. I wish I could just pause everything and have one real conversation, but that never seems to happen, and then I get annoyed with myself for not finding the right time. She texted me after, just a thumbs-up emoji, and I can’t tell if that means we’re okay or if she’s just tired too. There’s a mug with cold tea on the coffee table, and I keep forgetting to take it to the kitchen. I keep thinking I’ll fix things when I’m less rushed, but maybe that’s just another excuse. Need to get back to reading for class, but all I want to do is just sit here and figure out what to say next.

This morning, I spent way too long looking for my favorite black pen—ended up using a cheap blue one, which somehow threw me off for half the day. Now I’m on the bus home, watching the city lights blur past the window. My mind is jumping between the project feedback I got (not as bad as I expected, but still, could they be any vaguer?) and the argument I had with Jamie before leaving for work. I replayed the whole thing in my head so many times today, like if I analyze every word maybe I’ll find the right fix. It’s just so stupid how a little miscommunication can spiral. I keep wanting to text him, but then I chicken out because I’m not sure if it’ll make things better or just drag it out longer. The bus smells like wet pavement and someone’s leftover fast food, which isn’t helping my nerves settle down. I tried listening to a podcast but couldn’t focus on it for more than two minutes. Maybe I’ll just go home, eat cereal, and sketch until my brain runs out of steam. Honestly, I just wish things felt a little less jagged tonight.

Earlier today I remembered how I used to just buy that fancy bread at the grocery store without even thinking, but now I stood there comparing price tags like it was some kind of test. Tonight, after everyone was asleep and the house was quiet for once, I slipped on my shoes and took a loop around the block because my head felt full—too many lists, deadlines, receipts. The streetlights made weird shadows on the sidewalk and I kept replaying the conversation with my editor in my head, wondering if my pitch was actually as clear as I thought. I keep telling myself I can juggle all this—the invoices, the word count, the bills stacked on the counter—but my phone buzzed with a reminder about rent and suddenly I was counting days instead of steps. My fingers were cold even in my pockets but the air felt good, like it was pressing pause for a minute. I know optimism is my thing, but tonight I mostly felt practical, just trying to check off what I can and not drop any pieces. I wish work felt less like a treadmill and more like an open window. Maybe tomorrow I’ll find a little more breathing space.

The hum of the refrigerator is louder than usual tonight, or maybe I’m just more aware of it as I lean against the counter. The kitchen clock says 5:13 a.m., but the sky outside is still pitch black—my sense of time feels as scrambled as the eggs I made out of habit. I double checked the shared calendar twice before bed and again when I woke up, like it’s some kind of magical talisman that will keep the week from derailing. Coparenting is a hell of a logistical puzzle; I can’t help but wonder if I’m doing enough to hold up my end, or if I’m just treading water in a sea of recurring events and color-coded reminders.

Grad school assignments are piling up, which is almost funny at my age. I find myself questioning, not for the first time, what exactly I’m chasing here. Is it a second act, or just a way to stave off the feeling that I’m becoming irrelevant? There’s a pile of laundry in the next room, and I caught myself envying its simplicity—no existential angst, just dirty clothes waiting to be cleaned. Maybe that’s the trick: focus on the next small thing, one load at a time. I’m restless, but at least that means I’m not numb. Guess that counts for something.

I couldn’t find my headphones earlier, which made finishing up some work awkward with all the noise. Everyone is home, and it’s like every conversation is a little too loud. Late last night I tried to unwind on the couch, but my brother was already there binge-watching some series with the volume up. I asked if he could turn it down, but he just shot back that I’m always complaining lately.

I didn’t want to start something, so I just sat there, scrolling on my phone, not really paying attention to anything. The room felt crowded and tense even though it was just the two of us. I kept thinking about how we used to get along better, but maybe it’s just the stress of everyone being crammed into one house.

Eventually I gave up and went to bed, still kind of frustrated. Woke up feeling foggy, like I didn’t really sleep. I want to fix things but I’m not sure how to start. Wish I had more space to just breathe for a bit.

Earlier this morning I almost forgot where I’d left my keys—checked every pocket twice before realizing they were still in the front door. That’s been happening more lately, little things slipping my mind while I juggle a million tasks. Right now I’m parked in the lot outside the co-working space, engine off, laptop bag on the passenger seat, and my phone buzzing with Slack messages I’m pretending not to see for a few minutes. The sun’s just hitting the windshield, making this weird pattern on my dashboard, and my mind is already running through deadlines: client edits, invoices, updating my portfolio, answering a half-dozen emails that came in overnight from three time zones. Sometimes I wonder if working remotely is actually more freeing or just a different kind of hectic—I love the flexibility, but boundaries blur so fast. No commute sounds amazing until you realize you haven’t taken a real break in weeks, and breakfast is eaten with one hand on the keyboard. Today I’m supposed to finish a website mockup for a new client, but I keep thinking about that old project I never wrapped up. My notes are a mess, scattered between apps and sticky notes, and I can’t shake the feeling I’m missing something important. Still, despite the rush, I’m feeling oddly optimistic—maybe it’s the clear morning or just relief that I actually remembered my keys this time. I need to be more organized, but every system I try falls apart after a few days. The practical side of me says make a list; the spontaneous part wants to just dive in and handle things as they come. Maybe I’ll compromise and voice record a to-do list on my phone before heading in. For now, I’ll just take a deep breath, ignore the notifications, and enjoy this quiet moment in the car before the day gets away from me again.

Feeling heavy and a little numb tonight. The kitchen clock says 5:14 am and the fridge is humming louder than usual. I haven’t really slept, just drifted in and out, mind replaying yesterday’s phone call with my sister. She’s still upset about how I missed Mom’s appointment last week. I keep telling myself it wasn’t intentional—I just lost track, but I know she’s tired of hearing my excuses. I keep replaying her voice, sharp but tired, and I can’t stop wondering if I’m just letting everyone down lately.

I made toast but let it go cold, too busy staring at the steam from the kettle and overthinking everything. The empty chair at the kitchen table makes the place feel even quieter, and sometimes I feel like I’m rattling around in this apartment, echoing off the walls. I know I should reach out more, but something holds me back—maybe it’s guilt, maybe it’s fear of another argument or just not knowing what to say anymore.

My body feels worn out, shoulders tight and eyelids heavy, but my brain won’t shut up. Thoughts swirling about Mom’s health, my unemployment, and how distant I feel from everyone lately. It’s exhausting trying to be strong when every little thing seems to hit harder these days. I wish I knew how to fix things with my sister, or at least stop beating myself up over every mistake. Maybe tomorrow I’ll try calling her again, or maybe I’ll just let another day pass—sometimes it’s hard to tell which is worse.

persona.life_context: in school, balancing work and classes

journal_text: Just finished messaging Sam, trying to clear the air after our argument last night. The TV is on low in the background but I can barely focus on it; my head keeps replaying the whole thing. I know I get defensive when I’m tired and stretched thin between studying and taking care of Dad, but I don’t think Sam really sees how much I’m juggling. The couch feels lumpy tonight and I keep shifting around, not able to get comfortable, and I keep glancing at my textbooks on the coffee table—should be reading, but my mind is elsewhere. I keep analyzing what I said, wondering if I was unfair or if I just need more patience. The clock says it’s just after 9pm, but it feels much later. Wish I could just let things go, but I always end up digging into every detail. Relationships are more complicated lately, maybe because everything else feels so unsettled. I hope Sam responds soon so I can stop overthinking and actually get some work done tonight.

I can hear the hum of my laptop fan as I sit at my bedroom desk, finishing up another round of shift schedules. My phone keeps buzzing with messages from the team about shift swaps and coverage, and it feels like I’ve spent the whole evening answering them. The new inventory system rollout was supposed to make things easier, but now there are more questions from the night crew than before. It’s hard to keep everything straight when the notifications never stop.

Remote work was supposed to give me more control, but it’s like the workday just stretches out into the night. I caught myself snapping at Jen earlier when she asked if I could help with the dishes. I feel bad about that. We barely talked at dinner, mostly just sat in silence while I read emails on my phone. I know she’s frustrated with how distracted I am lately, but I don’t know how to switch off work when it’s always here.

I keep telling myself I’ll set better boundaries. Maybe tomorrow I’ll try leaving my phone in the other room after 8pm, at least for a night. Right now I just want the team to stop messaging for a couple hours so I can actually unwind. Even as I write this, I’m thinking about the morning’s call and whether I missed anything urgent. It’s exhausting, but I’m not sure what else to do.

Tired and restless, I just sat on the couch last night, feeling the day sitting heavy on my chest. I kept replaying that argument with Marco in my head, the way his tone set me off and how I probably snapped back too fast. I can't shake the feeling that I overreacted, but things have been so tense in the kitchen lately. Every order feels like a test, and I catch myself watching every ingredient, every ounce, thinking about the numbers more than the flavors. Maybe that's why I took it personal when he said we were moving too slow. I know everyone's stressed with the new food costs, but I want them to know I'm still giving everything even if the money is tight. It's like I keep trying to prove I'm still the leader, even when I feel unsure about where things are headed. There's this fear that if I don't keep it all together, I'll lose what little hold I have on the team. I wish I could just sit and talk honestly with them about how scared I am, but I don't want to look weak. I miss the days when cooking was just about the food, not bills and egos and all this pressure. I keep hoping tomorrow will feel different, that I won't wake up with this knot in my stomach. But tonight, it just feels like I'm falling behind on all fronts, and I don't really know where it's all going anymore. Maybe I just need a few hours of sleep to clear my head. Or maybe I need to figure out who I am when I'm not standing behind that stove.

Was just rearranging the cereal boxes again so I could see the whole counter. It’s late but the kitchen is the only place I can think. The dishwasher is still full from earlier and nobody bothered to run it, so I guess that’ll fall to me in the morning. I kept looking at the sticky note on the fridge with everyone’s appointments for the week and realized I never rescheduled my own dentist thing after last time’s conflict. Not sure if I’ll even get a chance with the way everyone’s calendars overlap.

Tomorrow I need to follow up on two project emails and check in with the team about the deadline, but I know my mom will probably ask me to drive my sibling to their class. I said I’d handle the groceries, but now I’m not sure when. My phone is full of reminders but I keep missing things. Every time I try to plan around work stuff, someone else’s needs get in the way. I keep worrying I’m forgetting something big, but all the little things are already piling up. It’s just been a lot of shifting things around in my head, but nothing actually gets finished.

The hum of the fridge is about the only sound in the apartment right now, mixed with the faint street noises leaking through the window. It’s a weird kind of quiet that makes everything feel heavier, or maybe that’s just how I am tonight. I was looking at my phone, trying to line up the co-parenting schedule for next week, and I realized I’d missed a message from her about switching a day. My head’s been so full lately that I honestly can’t remember if we talked about this before or if I just imagined agreeing to it.

When I called her to clear it up, I could hear how tired she sounded too, maybe even more than me. We ended up talking in circles for a while, both of us trying to sound patient but getting frustrated over which days we each had down. She brought up something about last month when I was late picking him up, and I felt this weird mix of guilt and irritation, because I thought we’d already moved past that. I kept apologizing, but I’m not sure she really believed I meant it, which is frustrating because I do. Sometimes I wonder if we’re ever both going to be on the same page about all this stuff, or if it’ll always feel like a negotiation.

I guess I’m just tired, and it’s easy to lose track of things when my days don’t have much structure. I know she’s got more on her plate than me, with work and everything, and I try to remind myself of that when we argue. Still, I wish we could communicate without both of us getting defensive. Maybe it would help if I actually started writing things down instead of just trying to remember everything in my head, but even that feels like another thing to add to the list.

Now it’s late and I’m too wired to sleep. I keep replaying the conversation, wondering if I could have handled it better or if it just is what it is. I still feel hopeful that things will get easier, that we’ll find a rhythm that doesn’t leave us both exhausted and second-guessing. For now, I just want to get some rest and hope tomorrow feels a little less scrambled.

persona.life_context: new city, still building a social circle

journal_text:
I woke up early today because I wanted to get a head start on some readings before my afternoon seminar, but all I could think about was the awkwardness that happened yesterday with the group project team. The kitchen was quiet except for the hum of the fridge and the way the faucet dripped, which probably made me overthink things more. I keep replaying the conversation in my head, especially when Aisha kind of dismissed my suggestion about splitting the presentation slides. I’m not sure if I came off too controlling, or if I was just trying to keep things on track. Sometimes I wonder if my need to organize clashes with how scattered I can get when I’m nervous around new people.

I know I’m still figuring out how to fit in here and it’s only been a couple of months, but it gets frustrating not having a solid group yet. This afternoon we’re supposed to meet again, and I want to approach things differently, maybe listen more and not jump to logistical talk right away. It’s a little exhausting to constantly analyze every interaction, but I guess it’s part of building new friendships as an adult. I’m actually looking forward to the seminar, at least there I can focus on the material instead of social dynamics for a while. On days like this, I really miss having familiar faces around who just get me without all the extra effort.

Just got on the bus after that interview. I keep replaying my answers in my head, like, did I sound too desperate when I talked about needing a flexible schedule? And I forgot to mention that thing about managing multiple projects, which is basically my whole life right now with juggling job hunting and co-parenting. My phone buzzed three times during the interview, probably the shared calendar going off, but I just ignored it and tried to focus. Honestly, I feel all over the place.

I keep thinking about the rest of the week and how I’m supposed to coordinate with my kid’s mom about drop-offs. She texted while I was waiting for the bus, asking if I could switch days. I said yes without really checking my own calendar, so now I need to figure out how that’s going to work with second interviews, if I even get one. It’s like my brain wants to plan but keeps short-circuiting. I’m hopeful something will come through job-wise, but I also feel like I’m missing things left and right. At least the bus is quiet right now. I’ll try to get my head together before I get home. Maybe tomorrow I’ll write a list or actually use those reminders I keep setting.

The WiFi at work kept dropping right in the middle of chats today, which meant I had to apologize for delays more than usual. I could feel my patience thinning, and I’m not sure if it was the tech or just me getting tired of being the messenger for issues I can’t control. On the bus ride home this afternoon, I found myself replaying the conversation I had with Connor about cleaning the kitchen. He sounded annoyed, I was trying to stay diplomatic, but honestly, I’m frustrated too. It’s like the more we try to coordinate schedules, the less time we actually spend just relaxing or having a real conversation. I caught myself wishing I lived alone, just for a moment, but then immediately felt guilty because I know I’d probably be lonely. Still, the tension is getting to me. I keep thinking if I just organized my calendar better, or made a cleaning chart, things would be smoother, but then I remember that people don’t really run on charts or reminders. Maybe I need to be more upfront about how much the mess bothers me, instead of making jokes or brushing it off. The funny thing is, I’m usually the one telling customers to communicate clearly and not let things fester, but apparently I need to take my own advice. At least the bus is almost at my stop. I’m hoping a quiet evening with some music will help me shake this restless feeling.

persona.life_context: new relationship, unsure where it is going

journal_text: Put down my sketchbook a few minutes ago and now just sitting here on the couch, staring at the ceiling. The apartment is quiet except for the hum of the fridge and some traffic outside, but my brain feels anything but quiet. Tried drawing something about how I feel but it came out disjointed, like I couldn’t even decide what the subject was supposed to be. She texted earlier, something about plans for the weekend, and I still haven’t replied. Not because I don’t want to, but because I actually don’t know what I want to say. Been thinking a lot about what it even means to be in a relationship again at this age. Part of me wants to just let things flow and stop overthinking, but then I get caught up in wondering if I’m just drifting or if I’m actually moving toward something real. It’s strange, I feel organized in my work, my art supplies all in place, my projects mapped out. But this other part of life feels messy and unresolved. I wish I could just ask her where she sees this going, but I know that’s not how these things work. Maybe I’ll answer her tomorrow, after some sleep. For now, I’ll just try to let the quiet settle in and hope I can actually rest tonight.

The hum of the fridge is the loudest thing in this break room, and the light here is sort of bluish, almost cold. Lunch was a quick sandwich I made at home, nothing fancy, but it was filling enough. I keep scrolling through my bank app, counting how much I have left for the week. It's not much, but I know I can stretch it if I pay attention. Sometimes I wonder if other students feel this anxious about money or if I just notice it more when I'm tired. Class tonight feels like a mountain, but it's one I have to climb. My notes are a mess, and I keep thinking I should organize them, just never seem to have the energy for it lately. Still, I want to believe all this work will mean something, even if I can't see the end yet. There are moments when I feel sure of myself, but today isn't really one of them. Maybe after class I'll try to read something for fun, just to remind myself I can. Hoping tomorrow is a little lighter, but for now, I'll finish this sandwich and get ready to go back.
